In a recent development, A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

In a recent development, each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

According to recent reports, the direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:.

The obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

It has been revealed that the first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

Sources indicate that the second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:.

According to recent reports, on a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a new connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

According to recent reports, A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a newly introduced connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

Node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for newly introduced connections, and the gateway did not.

The fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:.

According to recent reports, second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:.

We then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

Sources indicate that this advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

Each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

It has been revealed that for each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

The interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:.

An interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Recent findings suggest that every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:.

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:.

The machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

Industry observers note that liteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point reveals up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

Logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

If 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

In a recent development, before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

Industry observers note that the pages of a site form a graph. Think of it as many nodes connected to each other via edges. Each of the edges are the links between the pages, and the nodes themselves are the pages. Now if you start to visualize this as a graph, you will rapidly see that there are multiple ways to traverse this graph and reach a particular endpoint.

A search crawler usually uses one of these pages as a starting point and crawls through all of the pages (especially when pages are not fully covered in a sitemap).

If a page lies very deep from the home page, it means that it's not an key page. It's an indication to the search engine that this is not something that you yourself consider important, and the search engine has a lesser incentive to rank this page over pages that are linked better within your site.

Industry observers note that the key metric here is link depth. That is the number of clicks it takes to reach a particular page from your home page.

Sources indicate that another key metric is broken links. If you have too many broken links, it indicates to the search engine that your site is outdated and not well maintained, and the search engine will then not want to rank your site.

The way to identify both these problems is the same: to actually walk through your site, do a crawl of your site outside in, and try to figure out what the link depth is and if there are broken links on your website.

Seed the crawl with the home page and all URLs mentioned in the sitemap. Technically, the sitemap is not required if you're doing a crawl, but going from the sitemap will allow us to detect orphaned pages as well.

In a recent development, fetch the pages and follow redirects as required. Record when you're following a redirect: we do not let fetch follow it silently, we record each hop and add its target to the crawl. Record HTTP errors as they occur.

Drop URL fragments and tracking parameters. Keep trailing slashes because sometimes there can be mismatches around expectation of trailing slashes in different URLs of a site.

According to recent reports, in order to navigate from the home page, we can use BFS. So we know that the first time we reach a page, that is the page's shortest path.

We can cut off the depth over a certain threshold, say 5, to indicate that pages beyond that are too far or too deep to be reached.

Noindex pages will still be crawled. However, we need to make a record of them being not indexed, to reflect that they will not be present in the search engine.

Sources indicate that the desired page depth is as close to the home page as possible. Crucial pages should be close to the home page. The deeper you go from the home page, it signals to the search engine that the page is less important.

A couple of examples of how a deep page is present:.

The suggested fix for this is that we link the pages from as close to the home page as possible:.

Industry observers note that wasted links are those internal links that do not do the job they're supposed to do. The different types of wasted links:.

Sources indicate that we have seen here how to look at our own website through the lens of a search engine. You can use some of the code over here to create your own crawler and identify internal linking concerns; the full script is in this gist. Alternatively, we can use a free internal link visualizer to identify these issues and focus only on the fixes to improve our site's internal linking.

Google Voice app gets a redesign on Android, and it screams RCS [Gallery]

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a new app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a major neon sign that notes “RCS is coming.”.
  • It has been revealed that google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet.
  • That might finally be changing, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a new app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a major neon sign that notes “RCS is coming.”.

It has been revealed that google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet. No normal carrier, just an app tied to your Google account that gets a phone number with the ability to make calls and send/receive text messages. The latter, though, has been a point of contention for the past few years as Voice was excluded from Google’s huge push into RCS.

That might finally be changing, though. Recent updates brought mention of RCS in the app’s code.

Now, a slightly newer version (v2026-11-01-1019342246) of Google Voice has debuted a redesign for the app on Android.

It has been revealed that the new look isn’t a drastic restructuring, but a huge coat of paint on an app that hasn’t seen any meaningful updates since 2023. The new look feels more modern and very much influenced by Google Messages. The text field at the bottom has a rounded design with the same “+” and camera icons found in Messages, as well as a new long-press gesture that is, again, similar to Google’s primary messaging app. The main page hasn’t been updated beyond a new, rounded search bar up top and some subtly bolder fonts.

According to recent reports, material You colors are hit or miss now. On a Pixel with an orange theme, that color influenced the entire UI, but on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a coral/blue theme, the only sign of themeing was a blue message field.

The most notable thing here is the “SMS” icon on the send button, which looks just like the button in Google Messages. In that app, it’s used as an indicator as to what type of message you’re sending – SMS or RCS. Combined with code in that other recent upgrade directly pointing to “RCS” being used on a send button, you can absolutely tell Google Voice is finally adding this long-overdue functionality.

A timeline for RCS support in Google Voice is still unclear, but this redesign going live now certainly suggests it’s coming sooner rather than later.

Researchers are making Lego-like lunar dust bricks for building on the moon

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there are plenty of techno-fantasies about living on the moon, but what would these lunar cities actually be made from?
  • Industry observers note that there are plenty of techno-fantasies about living on the moon, but what would these lunar cities actually be made from?
  • Research from the University of Arkansas found that regolith, the loose lunar dust that covers the moon, could be used to 3D print Lego-like bricks that could one day be used in the construction of permanent structures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there are plenty of techno-fantasies about living on the moon, but what would these lunar cities actually be made from? Blasting concrete, rebar, and substantial, bulky construction equipment into space isn’t feasible, so some scientists are exploring how to build a base on the moon using what’s already up there: moon dust. Research from the University of Arkansas found that regolith, the loose lunar dust that covers the moon, could be used to 3D print Lego-like bricks that could one day be used in the construction of permanent structures. Their research, written up by Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering; Cole McCallum, then an undergraduate; and others, was published in NPJ Advance Manufacturing in August. [Photo: Cole McCallum/University of Arkansas] What makes 3D printing with locally available materials on the moon more difficult than on Earth is that the moon materials are harder to pack. This is because meteorites repeatedly crashing into Earth’s only natural satellite make its surface rough and jagged. There’s no wind or water to smooth things down, and nothing to bind the material together. “Lunar dust is essentially finely broken rock,” Shou tells Fast Manufacturer. “Unlike typical soil on Earth, it contains no organic matter from plants or other organisms.” Those irregular particles create a manufacturing challenge. They don’t spread and pack as evenly as the spherical powders commonly used in metal 3D printing, which makes it harder to produce uniform layers and consistent bonding. Instead of actual moon dust, researchers used commercially available lunar regolith simulant, a synthetic material that approximates the way real lunar dust looks and behaves. To form the bricks, they used a form of 3D printing called laser powder bed fusion in which a high-powered light or laser fuses a fine layer of powder through a process called sintering. The team tested different laser conditions, then built thicker, multilayer specimens before forming several small interlocking bricks. Other attempts to create building materials that would work with lunar dust have required additional binders, solvents, or processing materials. But the University of Arkansas researchers wanted to create with a method that was direct and binder-free so as to minimize the materials that would need to be transported from Earth. To build on the prototype, Shou indicates they need to improve the bonding between layers, reduce defects, improve the mechanical performance, and refine the surfaces so the bricks can fit together more securely. From there, the next steps would be testing fabrication in a vacuum and with low gravity, as well as testing durability through repeated temperature changes. “Making an interlocking brick is an encouraging first step,” Shou says. “A construction system will require predictable performance across both individual bricks and assembled structures.” Shou says they envision that in the future, there’s a possibility of using concentrated light directly to do a similar fabrication. If it works, that’s a simple recipe for a basic structure made from just two ingredients: a moon base made from moon dust and sunshine.

J.Crew’s upcoming Miles Davis capsule honors the jazz icon’s preppy style

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Miles Davis was arguably as famous for his fashion as he was for his music—American Ivy suits, African dashikis, and textured Issey Miyake shirts were all part of his wardrobe.
  • Miles Davis was arguably as famous for his fashion as he was for his music—American Ivy suits, African dashikis, and textured Issey Miyake shirts were all part of his wardrobe.
  • Sources indicate that now, 100 years after the artist’s birth, J.Crew has released a limited-edition capsule collection inspired by his legendary style and the American heritage look that is at J.Crew’s core.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Miles Davis was arguably as famous for his fashion as he was for his music—American Ivy suits, African dashikis, and textured Issey Miyake shirts were all part of his wardrobe. Now, 100 years after the artist’s birth, J.Crew has released a limited-edition capsule collection inspired by his legendary style and the American heritage look that is at J.Crew’s core. Released November 20, the collection includes a T-shirt, an Oxford shirt, and a baseball cap. “From his tailored suits and Ivy League-inspired wardrobe to the way he mixed classic pieces with a more individual, unconventional sensibility, Miles helped shape a look that continues to influence today,” states Golnar Khosrowshahi, founder and CEO of music rights firm Reservoir Media. (Reservoir acquired 90% of Davis’s music publishing catalog last year, alongside shared control of his name, image, and likeness). The lasting style is apparent in the capsule’s three objects. First, there’s a co-branded Oxford shirt, technically a J.Crew 1983, that is an homage to the mint-green button-down Davis wore on the cover of his 1958 album Milestones. To help the shirt hang just like the one on the album, J.Crew opted for a “heritage fit” that features a slightly longer collar and substantial weight from the 100% woven cotton, resulting in a relaxed take on the classic. Then there’s a vintage-wash cotton shirt emblazoned with an illustration of Davis. The reference image dates back to 1970, photographed by Glen Craig at a performance at the Fillmore East in New York City. Lastly, a classic black baseball cap is adorned with Davis’s signature, embroidered in vibrant blue thread against the rugged-wash canvas. The collection follows a series of limited-edition drops from J.Crew, which has partnered with the New York Fire Department and The New Yorker as part of the retailer’s broader post-bankruptcy strategy to be at the “center of culture.” “Collaborations create a meaningful entry point for people who may know Miles Davis well and are discovering J.Crew through the collection, while giving longtime J.Crew customers a new perspective on familiar pieces,” a J.Crew spokesperson tells Fast Company. “They help us keep our classics in the cultural conversation.” It’s not surprising that the clothing company would want to feature the most well-known jazz musician of the 20th century in its product line. But for Khosrowshahi, landing on J.Crew as a partner for Davis’s centennial celebration was a way of highlighting Davis’s legacy beyond music, focusing on fashion instead. “The goal isn’t to put an artist’s name on as many products as possible; it’s to find the right collaborators and create experiences that reflect the artist’s identity, values, and influence,” Khosrowshahi says. “This J.Crew collaboration is one example of how we’re bringing that broader vision to life.” The collection also brings Davis into the smaller details. The inside labels pair the J.Crew logo with a red silhouette of Davis playing the trumpet in place of the classic J.Crew Oarsman. The items’ tags also stand out for featuring Davis’s signature. The capsule is available online and at select J.Crew stores, including Bond Street, Rockefeller Center, and Fifth Avenue in New York City; Century City in Los Angeles; Newbury Street in Boston; North Michigan Avenue in Chicago; and Georgetown in Washington, D.C. “Preserving Miles’ legacy doesn’t mean keeping it frozen in time,” a spokesperson from the Miles Davis Estate says. “Miles was always looking ahead, always experimenting, and always pushing boundaries. Whether through music, fashion, visual art, or other creative collaborations, we want people to recognize just how far his influence extends.”.

#11772. Latest Update: How do brands measure customer experiences when AI does the shopping?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1840 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How do brands measure customer experiences when AI does the shopping?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Let’s take a step back to the dotcom era.
  • Let’s take a step back to the dotcom era.
  • As purchasing power shifts to artificial intelligence agents like Meta Muse, OpenAI Dots, and Instinct AI, consumers won’t navigate web pages and mobile applications; they’ll tell their digital proxies what they want and let the agent do the work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s take a step back to the dotcom era. When companies moved from brick and mortar to e-commerce, businesses scrambled to figure out CX strategies that would attract and retain customers online. Search engine optimization, cookies, and tech innovations swiftly followed to infer as much as possible about consumer intent, journeys, and experiences. Today, brands are still trying to understand these signals, but there’s a new twist. As purchasing power shifts to artificial intelligence agents like Meta Muse, OpenAI Dots, and Instinct AI, consumers won’t navigate web pages and mobile applications; they’ll tell their digital proxies what they want and let the agent do the work. This change will upend traditional notions of marketing, personalization, e-commerce, and customer experience. After a consumer agent interacts with a company, how will the company understand the experience? Why did the agent pick Store A versus Store B? Will the agent explain their decision process? How will the agent traverse digital assets? How much information will an agent share with companies during interactions? And how can a brand measure the customer’s “customer experience” when the buyer isn’t directly interacting with the brand? What Agents Mean for Consumers Customer experiences have endured seismic change over the past few decades. In the late 1990s, the dotcom era introduced digital disintermediation, and leaders like Amazon and Walmart leaped ahead of traditional department stores, specialty retailers, and shopping malls that failed to adapt their business models. Years later, as smartphones became pervasive, consumers moved to the new medium. Successful organizations adopted unified customer profiles across devices, geolocation and tracking technologies, and even more surgically precise personalization to create more relevant, quality experiences. Agentic commerce will drive another CX revolution across marketing, sales, and service. But to understand how companies should respond, we need to start with what this shift means for consumers. A personalized AI agent can do more. While an agent is powered by the same underlying technology that drives large language models like Gemini and Claude, it does more than answer questions or make recommendations. When you ask an agent to do something, it interviews you to understand your preferences and remembers past experiences. It takes the initiative to scour the internet, make calls, comparison shop, make reservations, order deliveries, and call or chat with customer support on your behalf to make sure you get what you want. You tell it what you want, and it does the work. As consumers embrace personal agents, this convenience means people will spend less time and effort shopping, buying, and interacting with brands. The traditional omni-channel, customer-led journey—reading reviews, shopping online, and dealing with a mix of chatbots, voice bots, and frontline employees— will be driven less by the consumer and more by the agent. Understanding and establishing customer satisfaction, loyalty, and brand equity will require new tools and techniques. What Agents Mean for Brands We’re just beginning this transition to an agentic experience. When agents mediate product discovery and purchasing decisions on a customer’s behalf, data and signals showing whether the interaction drove the desired outcomes are obscured. That requires a better understanding of what happens during agentic interactions themselves. The CX business was built on surveys and scores like the Net Promoter Score (NPS). But NPS has always been a proxy for how likely a customer is to do business with a brand again. Real loyalty measures are behavioral, like how recently they engaged with the brand, the quality of the interaction, or how consistently they spent with the company. Traditional measures like those work when customers can directly reflect on an interaction, but they don’t tell the whole story when AI agents handle it. Brands still need to distinguish between completing a transaction and meeting the customer’s needs. Without connecting signals, businesses can lose sight of the overall relationship. What Brands Can Do About It As with any disruptive technology, we will see some businesses adapt to this new era of personalized agents more successfully than others. Companies will face the challenge of learning how to optimize their business model to work with agents without compromising the quality and efficiency of an evolving customer experience. Agents may not need to share customer preferences or details with companies to be effective, but organizations should create incentives for them to do so. Today, a customer who provides a rewards number can earn rewards. With the right incentives, customer agents should still do so. Brands should build corporate agents that can communicate richly and honestly with customer agents. Agents, like humans, thrive on information. The more information a corporate agent exchanges with a customer agent, the better the agents can make informed, relevant decisions. The key is to listen everywhere. Don’t treat this new channel as if it doesn’t have context. Connect customer agentic interactions with digital, conversational, and in-person interactions into journeys and outcomes. By doing so, organizations can uncover critical insights, interests, and motivations that would otherwise remain hidden within the agentic black box. The New CX New technology often creates uncertainty. Think of when music moved from physical discs to digital platforms like iTunes or Spotify. Some record labels resisted giving up the physical relationship they built with fans, but eventually, to be relevant, labels embraced the new media. Brands may see agentic commerce as a similar threat to customer experience control. But brands that leverage these new channels to build relationships with new and existing customers will find that AI agents present a tremendous opportunity for insight rather than an existential threat.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xiaomi is pushing the limits of modern smartphone specs with a killer design, flush camera lenses, and a next-gen Snapdragon SoC.

If you’re looking for a phone with top-tier specs, Xiaomi has a upcoming phone for you. The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max are the company’s latest flagships, available starting today, November 17. When looking at the spec list for the Xiaomi 18 series, it’s difficult to find anything that was left out.

During the launch presentation, Xiaomi emphasized that its new privacy display wasn’t just a copy of “other privacy displays.” Rather, they created an entirely new subpixel layout called HyperRGB 2.0 that delivers far higher resolution and brightness output than the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. You can also enable and disable the privacy display feature on the Xiaomi 18 Pro series with a click of the new AI button on the left side of the phone. Functionally, Xiaomi’s privacy display looks nearly identical to Samsung’s, including the ability to have specific apps use it.

Both models feature identical specs, including the privacy display and cameras, with the exception of the screen size, battery capacity, and charging speed. Here are the differences:.

Recent findings suggest that the 120Hz LTPO display is bordered by a 0.99mm bezel, the smallest in the industry so far, 4,000-nit peak brightness, and TÜV Rheinland Triple Eye Care Certification, including a 2160Hz PWM dimming rate. Inside the phone is a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 processor with a 3D IceLoop cooling system, and each model’s silicon-carbon battery includes 28% silicon content.

On the back is a pair of 200MP cameras, including a 1/1.28-inch main sensor and a 1/1.56-inch periscope telephoto sensor. These are massive sensors, especially compared to the 1/3.94″ and 1/2.52″ telephoto sensors in the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Despite their size, Xiaomi packs them onto the back in an island with fully flat glass — no protruding camera lenses!

That island on the back isn’t just for cameras, though. It also packs in a 120Hz LTPO M11 OLED panel with 4,000-nit peak brightness for ultra-high-quality selfies and group shots, plus support for notifications and apps. Xiaomi created a latest GenAI Apps feature that lets you create your own apps on the back display, plus official support for several popular apps like Google Maps, Spotify, and more.

Industry observers note that the Xiaomi 18 Pro series ships with HyperOS 4 (Android 17) and includes 3 months of Google AI Pro, plus 5TB of Google Cloud storage. The Xiaomi 18 Pro retails for €1399 for the model with 12GB RAM and 256GB storage, or €1599 for 12GB/512GB. The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max starts at €1599 for 12GB/256GB, €1799 for 12GB/512GB, and a 16GB/1TB model will be available soon for €2099.

It has been revealed that some retailers also sell a bundle that includes the Official silicone magnetic case, which usually retails for €39, as well as the Magnetic Remote Stand, which retails for €69. That remote stand functions as a MagSafe-style stand and remote, giving you camera shutter functionality and a scrolling feature.

How Anthropic believes branding will shape its post-IPO future

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that anthropic enjoyed a singularly blockbuster debut on the Nasdaq yesterday, shrugging off any concerns about going public at a moment when the artificial intelligence industry faces a strained public image.
  • It has been revealed that anthropic enjoyed a singularly blockbuster debut on the Nasdaq yesterday, shrugging off any concerns about going public at a moment when the artificial intelligence industry faces a strained public image.
  • Investors are fundamentally betting on the technology underpinning Anthropic’s products and business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that anthropic enjoyed a singularly blockbuster debut on the Nasdaq yesterday, shrugging off any concerns about going public at a moment when the artificial intelligence industry faces a strained public image. ANT priced at $83 a share, above expectations, making it the biggest IPO of all time, worth a staggering $1.5 trillion; it finished its first trading day at $97.17. Investors are fundamentally betting on the technology underpinning Anthropic’s products and business. But in this case, it’s easy to overlook the importance of another factor that’s played a major role in the company’s remarkable rise: strong brand optics. Anthropic itself makes that case in its S-1 form, which gave investors a glimpse into the company’s thinking before its IPO. Tellingly, the word “brand” appears 63 times. Admittedly, the S-1 is a book-length document covering many topics. But the filing reveals a company that recognizes how much branding has mattered in a razor-competitive category like AI—and how much it will matter in the future. Many of Anthropic’s rivals have launched on the backs of widely known brands or brand ecosystems: Google’s Gemini, Meta’s Muse, Elon Musk’s Grok, Microsoft’s Copilot. OpenAI became a household name thanks to the surprise popularity of its ChatGPT product, and an avalanche of publicity. Anthropic, by contrast, didn’t even exist until a few years ago, when a group broke away from OpenAI to found what was then an upstart rival. With a story specifically touting ethical responsibility and social trust, it leaned on a brand-forward identity from the start. With notable exceptions—Apple especially—tech companies often treat branding as a squishy afterthought. Innovation and word of mouth, the thinking goes, drive success, not a promoted public image. Anthropic, no doubt, attributes its rapidly growing profile to its flagship chatbot, Claude, and other products establishing it as a world-class AI lab with enormous upside potential (and similarly extreme risks). [Photo: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images] But it’s worth unpacking what that filing had to say on the subject of growth. It argues that even a category-leading product depends on brand reputation, and offers insight into how Anthropic will pursue its branding goals after the IPO. Building on its founding proposition as the AI company with a conscience, Anthropic seeks to cement an image that commingles efficiency and trust, leveraging individual connection with its products to fuel enterprise growth. For starters, Anthropic reports that its annual ad spending spiked from $33 million in 2024 to $147 million last year, and is expected to keep growing in 2026. (Notably, Anthropic advertised during the Super Bowl this year, poking at OpenAI for incorporating ads into its chat results.) That may not sound like much for a company that reported $33 billion in revenue through the first nine months of 2026, but it’s clear that its brand strategy isn’t just a gloss, and in fact will help drive growth. “The promotion of our brand requires us to make substantial expenditures, which we anticipate will increase as our market becomes more competitive,” the filing explains. “If we do not successfully maintain and enhance our brand, our business may not grow, we may have reduced pricing power relative to competitors, we could lose customers.” More specifically, Anthropic positions brand building as a way to become a recognizable, deliberately chosen collaborator to what it dubs “prosumers.” These individuals pay for AI tools to perform knowledge work and their personal product preferences can influence organizational purchasing like, say, bringing Claude into their workplaces. The filing doesn’t quite suggest that Anthropic thinks models are becoming commodities, or that branding will ultimately matter more than performance. But in effect, it argues that in an increasingly competitive market, the brand is going to matter a lot to consumers (or prosumers) who see rival products as somewhat interchangeable, and find it easy to jump from one to another. [Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images] And maybe more to the point: Many others see AI as a problem, spawning controversial data centers and threatening jobs. As the S-1 cautions, Anthropic’s brand must also contend with “broader public perceptions of the AI industry, and we may be grouped with other industry participants and judged similarly, regardless of differences in our approach or conduct.”  The period just before Anthropic’s IPO was a rough stretch for the industry overall. It featured the Jensen Huang scandal at AI mainstay Nvidia, multiple air traffic and Internet failures that sparked (seemingly evidence-less) conspiracy theories centered on AI, and a handy New York Post quiz about surviving an “AI apocalypse.” Thus Anthropic has been at pains to distinguish itself as the cautious and thoughtful AI company, clashing with the Pentagon about military uses of its technology, claiming to want more regulation, keeping advertising out of its products—and going public as a public benefit corporation, a structure meant to prod leadership to think beyond profits. Not everyone is convinced. Critics accuse Anthropic leadership of having a “savior complex.” But it does seem remarkable that its IPO was such a roaring success despite a terrible stretch for the sector overall. The stock market measures investor sentiment, which is not quite the same as brand reputation—but also not totally unrelated. Anthropic’s brand may have aided its IPO’s success. And that success is certainly good for the brand.

#11768. 5 major network outages in three days: It’s not a conspiracy; it’s change

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2372 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

5 major network outages in three days: It’s not a conspiracy; it’s change

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, like millions of other Americans, I was stuck at an airport on the infamous Friday the 13th in November when air traffic in the U.S.
  • It has been revealed that like millions of other Americans, I was stuck at an airport on the infamous Friday the 13th in November when air traffic in the U.S.
  • In a recent development, that’s what happens when major networks go down: chaos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, like millions of other Americans, I was stuck at an airport on the infamous Friday the 13th in November when air traffic in the U.S. came to a halt. From where I sat at Fort Lauderdale airport, the panic was obvious. Crowds overflowed at gates. Hotel rooms disappeared swiftly. I got one of the last ones available in the city. It was chaos. That’s what happens when big networks go down: chaos. And it’s only just beginning unless organizations fix how they change their network infrastructures. Of course, the ground stop would have made news by itself. But what really got people talking was that it was one of a series of major outages that occurred over just a few days’ time. Shortly before the ground stop, a Microsoft Outlook outage left businesses unable to send email. Our company had contracts held up by it. And on Monday, November 16, customers at several major banks found they couldn’t reach their accounts. Email, air travel, banking—three essential elements of the American economy, not to mention people’s daily lives—crashed in the span of just three business days. Suddenly, people who don’t know a router from a switch were talking about network infrastructure. Conspiracy theories multiplied on social media and in the dark corners of the internet. I spend my working life close to the networks behind failures like these, and I can say with complete confidence that there is no conspiracy here. The root cause of all the outages might sound less satisfying than a complex conspiracy theory, but it is daunting nonetheless: The infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change always brings risk. When organizations fail to manage changes in their network infrastructure, the result, as we all saw last week, can be chaos. It almost always starts with a change The issue at the root of network outages is almost always change. Based on what we know at this point, change was at the root of the air traffic control failure. The network that carries communications between the major air traffic control centers is decades old and in the middle of a long modernization, which involves moving from legacy protocols and transmission to modern fiber and latest equipment. At one step of that transition, when new network devices were introduced, something went wrong. A misconfiguration or a misbehaving device sent traffic into the network that other devices couldn’t handle. Those devices began to fail, and the failure cascaded. Shortly after, the rush to find a hotel room began. The Outlook outage had the same origin: configuration changes, unintended consequences, knock-on failures. Some of the triggering configurations were already months old and sat quietly until a condition in the network finally exposed them. Why can’t networks just heal themselves? So, why do these outages occur? Networks are supposed to route around damage. In theory, they should. But in practice, change can shake up a network infrastructure in unpredictable ways. A network is, by definition, a set of interacting systems. Change one element and you change how its neighbors behave, and how their neighbors behave after that. Change is necessary. Unfortunately, it’s not always good, and when it’s bad it just gets worse as it travels through the network infrastructure. That’s why the teams who run critical networks practice serious discipline before a change: pre-change testing, a mapped-out plan for every step, a rollback plan. I’m confident the people involved last week did all of that. But the interconnections inside a large network are so vast that no team can test for every eventuality. That’s not carelessness. It’s the nature of complex, interconnected systems. It could happen to even the most prepared team. Redundancy helps, and these networks have layers of it. But redundancy does not remove complexity. In some ways, it adds to it. Why recovery takes so long So if a change caused the problem, the simple solution is to undo the change. But that’s not easy to do because the same interconnectedness that caused the failure makes it hard to reverse. A problem becomes exponentially more difficult to fix as it cascades through the network infrastructure and tangles itself into a complex web of systems. Here’s what has to happen for a team to fix an issue related to change: The team has to diagnose it. When effects cascade across the network, often it’s not obvious which change caused which symptom. This is where visibility becomes critical. You can’t fix what you can’t see. An accurate picture of the network, what’s connected to what, how each element should be configured, and what is happening right now can make the difference between a fast fix and one that takes many times longer while the team works in the dark. The team has to remediate, and rollback is just the start. By the time the team finds a cause, the problem has usually triggered other failures. Elements of the network infrastructure have to talk to one another again before the network works as it should. That process often has to happen in a careful order so the applications on top return cleanly. Microsoft’s team reportedly spent days painstakingly rebuilding its environment to avoid further knock-on effects. The team has to regain confidence that the problem won’t come straight back. The initial fix doesn’t always work. And when lives depend on the answer, caution is always the right call. I compare this process to heart surgery on a global stage. Teams get it right 99.99% of the time, but almost nobody notices. Their effort is monumental and continuous but largely anonymous. But when there is an outage, they are doing delicate, high-stakes work while the public watches the departure boards. Get used to network outages However, we’re about to hear a lot more about these teams because the rate of change in our infrastructure is rapidly accelerating. There are three reasons why: Decades-old systems are hitting their limits and must be modernized, as is the case with air traffic control. Modernization requires change, and change always involves risk. AI is putting new demands on networks. Agents and AI-powered applications are doing real work, and that work runs over infrastructure that can’t adequately carry it without growth and adaptation. AI brings a whole new set of security implications. This reason is the most urgent of the three. In my industry, we talk about the “patchpocalypse.” AI is helping uncover vulnerabilities faster than ever, some of which have been hidden for years or even decades. The time between discovery and exploitation has shrunk from a quarter or a year to mere hours. Every patch is a change to the network, and every change carries risk. Put all of those factors together, and you get infrastructure that’s 30 or 40 years out of date and needs to change almost immediately. The networks themselves aren’t necessarily more fragile, but their criticality, complexity, and necessity for change are all growing faster than teams and funding can keep up. Everything is going to feel shaky for a while. What IT leaders should do now Many of the world’s most crucial networks are still managed largely by hand, with limited data, limited visibility, and limited tooling for governing change. That approach isn’t sustainable anymore. IT leaders need to make two critical investments: Give your teams real data about their infrastructure. They should know what the network is, how it’s interconnected, how it’s meant to be configured, and what’s happening on it right now. In a crisis, they should see at a glance the impact, the affected workloads, the change that likely caused it, and the downstream effects. When speed is essential, visibility is critical. Finding a problem is a major step toward solving it. Govern change before it reaches the network. Change drove all the high-profile outages in mid-November 2026. Teams need to understand the risk and behavior of a change before they make it. Modern patch windows are measured in hours rather than months. Teams need to build discipline into tools and processes. The people running these networks are doing extraordinary work under extraordinary pressure with very little credit or recognition. The November outages demonstrate how much of the world’s economy and people’s daily lives depend on them. They deserve the data and the tools they need to keep networks running and avoid chaos.

Running an AI agent on your own GPU sounds simple: point it at Ollama and stop paying per token. I set up OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, with a 9B model in Ollama on one RTX 3090 and connected it to Discord. Then I read the Ollama log for every request.

It has been revealed that the agent worked. The numbers were not what I expected, though. A one-line question turned into a prompt of more than 18,000 tokens, the first reply took over a minute, and the small model sometimes guessed instead of using its tools.

This article covers what I measured and what each number means if you strategy to run an agent on local hardware.

Industry observers note that openClaw ran in Docker and reached Ollama on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434. Discord was the chat interface, and OpenClaw's web panel showed the sessions and context use.

According to recent reports, this article is about the results, not the installation. The full step-by-step setup is in a separate guide to running OpenClaw in Docker with Ollama and Discord. That guide covers the Compose file, the Discord bot and how to keep the ports off your network.

All timings below come from the Ollama log on the test machine. Ollama loaded the model with a 32,768-token context.

My first message in Discord was short: "Which model are you running on, and what is 17 * 23?" The bot answered correctly: it ran on ollama/qwen3.5:9b, and 17 × 23 is 391.

Industry observers note that the Ollama log showed what that question cost. The model processed 18,415 prompt tokens and generated 33 tokens.

Industry observers note that the extra tokens come from the agent itself. With every request, OpenClaw sends:.

According to recent reports, on the RTX 3090, reading that prompt took 10 seconds at 1,838 tokens per second. A slower GPU, or a CPU, needs much longer to read the same prompt.

Prompt tokens per model call, from the Ollama log. Only the first message had to process the whole prompt.

Sources indicate that openClaw counts tokens with its own estimate, which was higher than the Ollama count. The gateway log estimated the prompt at 24,608 tokens, against a prompt budget of 24,576 tokens for this model. By OpenClaw's own count, the base prompt alone used up the budget before any conversation history.

The web panel showed a similar figure: 68 to 69 percent of the context window was in use for the Discord sessions after only a few messages.

According to recent reports, the first message arrived while the model was not loaded in GPU memory. That reply took 1 min 10 s:.

The next requests were much faster:.

In a recent development, reply times on the test machine. Loading the model took most of the first reply.

It has been revealed that the speed-up comes from prompt caching. The system prompt, tool definitions and workspace files at the start of the prompt stay the same between requests. Ollama kept that part cached and processed only the newly introduced tokens. The model wrote at 91 to 96 tokens per second in every test.

According to recent reports, ollama's documentation indicates models stay in memory for 5 minutes by default before they are unloaded. After that, the next message pays the load time again. You can change this with the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE environment variable on the Ollama server, or with the keep_alive parameter per request. A negative value, such as -1, keeps the model loaded. I did not change this setting in the test.

If you run Ollama in Docker, pass the variable with -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 or in the environment: section of your Compose file.

Two things used the GPU besides my chat messages.

Recent findings suggest that A heartbeat. OpenClaw's web panel listed one scheduled automation, heartbeat-main, which runs every 30 minutes. The agent wakes on that schedule, so the model gets called even when nobody chats. With Ollama's 5-minute default, the model is unloaded between heartbeats unless someone chatted recently, so a heartbeat most likely starts with a model load. I did not measure this.

Industry observers note that an embedding model. During the first message, OpenClaw also called Ollama's /api/embed endpoint twice to index its memory. It used qwen3-embedding:4b, which was already installed on the Ollama server. I did not set OpenClaw to use that model; it picked it on its own.

The two models took this much GPU memory:.

That is 11.4 GB for the models alone, almost half of the RTX 3090's 24 GB.

The rest of the stack was light:.

It has been revealed that what this means for you: plan GPU memory for the chat model, the embedding model and the context, not the chat model alone. If the GPU also runs other models, the heartbeat can compete with them.

The first two tests in Discord: a question, then a file written with a tool. The user name is blurred.

The mistakes showed up when the model had to check something:.

After the restart, the bot claimed it had lost the earlier session. When asked to use its read tool, it read the file correctly.

The fix for the first problem was simple. When I wrote "use your read tool to open homelab-test.md", the model opened the file and listed all three points correctly. Naming the tool made it check instead of guess.

The model listed four files and missed the test file and a folder, because it answered from its prompt.

Based on this test, a local 9B model on one consumer GPU works for:.

If you need better answers, OpenClaw also works with hosted models, but then your prompts leave your machine.

It has been revealed that in this test, qwen3.5:9b used 6.3 GB and the qwen3-embedding:4b memory model used 5.1 GB. Together the two models needed 11.4 GB.

The model had to load into GPU memory first, which took 59 seconds of the 70-second reply. Ollama keeps a model loaded for 5 minutes by default, and the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE setting changes that.

It has been revealed that every request includes OpenClaw's system prompt, its tool definitions and its workspace files. A one-line question became an 18,415-token prompt in this test.

Sources indicate that yes. A heartbeat automation runs every 30 minutes and calls the model even when nobody sends a message.

It handled questions, arithmetic and file creation correctly in this test. It sometimes answered from its prompt instead of using its tools. When it wrongly mentioned its memory was lost, asking it to use its read tool made it check the file and answer correctly.

This holiday season, the best meal deals come with a side of merch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, socks aren’t usually something kids want for Christmas.
  • In a recent development, socks aren’t usually something kids want for Christmas.
  • According to recent reports, instead of a plastic toy, the chain is offering free pairs of ugly Christmas socks with every purchase of its Home Alone-themed specialty meal, which will arrive in stores December 1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, socks aren’t usually something kids want for Christmas. McDonald’s is betting adults will want them with their meal, though. Instead of a plastic toy, the chain is offering free pairs of ugly Christmas socks with every purchase of its Home Alone-themed specialty meal, which will arrive in stores December 1. With each order, customers will get one of four pairs of festive socks featuring illustrations of McDonald’s characters like Grimace, or Macaulay Culkin’s Home Alone character, Kevin McCallister. [Photo: McDonald’s] McDonald’s isn’t alone in this. The socks, designed in the style of an ugly Christmas sweater, are kitschy collectibles that fit within the broader trend of apparel releases by food and quick service brands, and it’s bigger than ever this holiday season. Burger King and Wendy’s are also giving away cold weather gear —both happen to be beanies, and Burger King’s is Peanuts-themed—with their holiday meal deals this year, too. [Image: Burger King] Restaurants and food brands have turned to clothing and apparel in recent years to capitalize on “post-ironic” cultural relevance and to deepen brand affinity even as shoppers pull back on spending. Chains like Cava have released their own ingredient-themed apparel collections, while other brands have turned to unconventional partnerships, like PringlesCrocs or Hidden Valley Ranch-flavored chapstick. For some fans, restaurant merch has become the fresh band T-shirt. [Photo: Wendy’s] The happy-meal-toys-for-adults trend also comes as grown-ups are increasingly ordering kids meals, according to the market research firm Circana, which found adult orders of kids meals are up 28% since 2019. At Burger King, the No. 2 U.S. burger chain by sales behind McDonald’s, sales of its King Jr. meal are up 40% year over year, which the chain attributes in part to more adult purchases with no kids around. [Photo: Wendy’s] Designing a kids meal for adults, then, is catering to an already growing customer base. Instead of giving them toys with their meals, apparel is a giveaway that’s usable. Due to rising prices, customers have dined out less frequently over the past two years; to win them back, chains are focusing on quality and value. Though McDonald’s has fared better than many of its competitors, it unveiled a 0.2% decline in U.S. sales on its earnings call this month. To grow its domestic business, the chain is rolling out new menu items with smaller portion sizes and more protein, as well as leaning into specialty drinks and dirty sodas. Meals themed around nostalgic IP like Home Alone add up to another tactic. [Photo: McDonald’s] McDonald’s is marketing the meal as an invitation to “leave adulthood behind” by tapping into nostalgia, and letting the customers customize their meals by picking their own entrée. It also leans into Home Alone through its menu items: french fries rebranded as “Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries” for the film’s fictional pizza chain, along with a McFlurry, and pizza-flavored seasoning packet and dipping sauce. This is what a kids meal looks like when it’s “kidulting.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that bally's North America Interactive unit grew revenue 25.6% in the third quarter of 2026, well ahead of a slowing US iGaming market, and narrowed its segment loss.
  • Bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter.
  • The pace stands out against the wider market.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that bally's North America Interactive unit grew revenue 25.6% in the third quarter of 2026, well ahead of a slowing US iGaming market, and narrowed its segment loss. The online unit still lost money, and the results came with another delayed quarterly filing after a going-concern warning in August.

Bally’s online business in the United States and Canada grew faster than the market in the third quarter. It is still not profitable. North America Interactive groups the manufacturer’s sports betting and iGaming businesses in both countries. The unit lost less money than a year earlier, but it stayed in the red.

The pace stands out against the wider market. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, according to Citizens JMP Securities. That was down from 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. Bally’s online growth ran well ahead of that slowing trend.

The quarter was not a clean step up, though. North America Interactive posted $66.1 million in second-quarter revenue, up 16.9% from a year earlier. Third-quarter sales were therefore lower than the quarter before. First-quarter revenue was $60.5 million, a 35.9% increase.

For the first nine months of 2026, the unit had preliminary revenue of $189.2 million. That compares with $134.0 million for February 8 to September 30, 2025, and $16.9 million for January 1 to February 7, 2025.

A narrower loss points to progress. Yet the unit has not reached break-even, even while growing faster than the market. For a smaller US operator, online scale is still not translating into profit.

In a recent development, all third-quarter figures are preliminary. Bally’s has not finished closing its books for the period ended September 30, 2026, and the numbers could change. It filed a late-filing notice dated November 10 because it needed more time to finish reviewing its third-quarter financial statements.

Recent findings suggest that that makes three late quarterly reports in 2026. Bally’s notified the SEC in May that its first-quarter report would be late. It did the same in August for the second quarter. Both notices cited more time needed to review financial statements.

In the first-quarter 10-Q, management concluded that disclosure controls were not effective. The cause was a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting, first disclosed in the 2025 annual report.

The second-quarter 10-Q, filed August 14, went further. Two tests tied to the tech giant’s revolver, a net leverage covenant and a liquidity requirement, were expected to be missed during the coming year. That same filing carried a going-concern warning, questioning whether Bally’s could keep operating. The shares fell more than 25% in one trading session afterward.

Recent findings suggest that bally’s reports strong revenue growth in Q3 2026. Data and info: https://t.co/ekSd5Ngu0Q.

• Group revenue increased 22% to USD 807.6m, while North America Interactive revenue rose 26% to USD 62.7m.

— OGQ-Magazine (Online Gambling Quarterly) (@OGQMagazine) November 10, 2026.

CEO Robeson Reeves said development projects remain on track and market conditions are stable going into the fourth quarter and 2027. The Bronx casino resort is expected to cost $4.0 billion and open by 2030. Bally’s closed a financing package led by WhiteHawk Capital Partners that provided $400 million in term loans for the project. Another $160 million in delayed-draw commitments remains available. The term loans come due 18 months after they are first funded.

The delayed third-quarter 10-Q comes next. The firm has mentioned it should arrive before its five-day SEC grace period runs out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that starbucks obviously knows coffee, but the chain has also mastered the ability to sell endlessly collectible merchandise. Collecting its mugs and cold cups has been a hobby of die-hard fans and online content creators who make videos about hunting for the latest drop, and interest in Starbucks merchandise reaches a fever pitch around the holidays. In November 2025, the company introduced the Starbucks Bearista Glass Cold Cup in the U.S. The handblown, bear-shaped glass cup for cold drinks came with a Starbucks-green beanie and a green-and-white striped straw that proved irresistible. Lines snaked around stores before their early-morning openings. More than one store witnessed physical fights, and videos on social media of people “hunting” the cup racked up views. The Bearista has been a recurring mascot for the brand since 1997, when Starbucks introduced a plush, green-aproned bear for the holidays. In 2023, it morphed into a cold cup in Korea, then spread throughout Asia before hitting the U.S. last November. By then it was already on cup collectors’ radars. Dana Pellicano, SVP of global product experience, Starbucks: We were seeing this trend of kidulting, adults leaning into playful, fun products. The confluence of that, [the bear’s legacy], and the rise of cold drinks made it the right time for us to bring it to the U.S. Carol Casey, aka RayahSunshine, cup collector/content creator: In the cup community, we see lots of cups coming out of other countries that are really enticing. We noticed that Starbucks Asia had a very unique set of cups. Their cups were more cutesy. The artisan quality of the cup meant its supply was very limited. That created demand for social media videos of how to find one, and even created a secondary market on eBay. In a statement, the company apologized to those who weren’t able to snag one. Pellicano: What makes it special is also what makes it logistically hard and part of the reason we had to be really disciplined about how we introduced it. When you say yes to something, you’re saying no to something else. So we are saying yes to this really premium, elevated offering and therefore unintentionally saying no to everybody being able to have one. These are the choices that you have to balance. Lindsay Ream, Starbucks coffeehouse leader, Grand Rapids, Michigan: Everybody wanted it. We get to the store at 4 a.m.—we open at 4:30—and when we got here, we had six cars in the parking lot waiting for us to open the doors. All day long the phone rang. We had someone answering all day to say “sorry, we’re sold out.” Casey: Because stores stagger their openings and resellers pop from store to store, it’s very competitive. I like to go where I know I can for sure get the cup. With the limited editions, you’re there at 3 a.m., and some people were getting there at 2. The Bearista bear went nuts. Everybody was trying to get it—and people were willing to spend $250 on eBay for it. It was so limited that it upset people more than not, but it did bring a lot of interest. Since last year, Starbucks has launched four more Bearista cups—the Pink Drink Bearista with a white hat and strawberry straw topper, an online-exclusive, soccer-themed Bearista for Starbucks Rewards Reserve tier members, and a Snoopy-shaped cup for fall. For the holiday season, the original Bearista is making a comeback, with a surprise box that contains one of four variations on the original, with the potential to include a rare golden Bearista.. Pellicano: We’ve really worked to refine our processes, and we’ve had a lot of success. We try to match the natural demand of where our stores see real volume in driving merch. We capped how many cups customers can purchase [at two per person]. Ream: In my district, we talked about partners not buying cups ahead of time. We have “partner access” where employees only were offered an early launch, but it didn’t come out of the amount of cups that we had for customers. Casey: I may hunt it [again] just for the sake of the hunt and the content—just because that’s what I do.

For the holiday season, the original Bearista is making a comeback, with a surprise box that contains one of four variations on the original, with the potential to include a rare golden Bearista..

Industry observers note that pellicano: We’ve really worked to refine our processes, and we’ve had a lot of success. We try to match the natural demand of where our stores see real volume in driving merch. We capped how many cups customers can purchase [at two per person].

Ream: In my district, we talked about partners not buying cups ahead of time. We have “partner access” where employees only were offered an early launch, but it didn’t come out of the amount of cups that we had for customers.

Casey: I may hunt it [again] just for the sake of the hunt and the content—just because that’s what I do.

I voiced a character in ‘Grand Theft Auto.’ I never expected her to follow me for 17 years

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI generated more than $1.65 billion in preorder sales, broke internet usage records, and shattered streaming records on platforms like Twitch and YouTube.
  • The release of Grand Theft Auto VI generated more than $1.65 billion in preorder sales, broke internet usage records, and shattered streaming records on platforms like Twitch and YouTube.
  • Sources indicate that for me, as someone who works in digital editorial and audience engagement for a media manufacturer that covers tech and news, the data is staggering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI generated more than $1.65 billion in preorder sales, broke internet usage records, and shattered streaming records on platforms like Twitch and YouTube. For millennials who played video games growing up, this is a cultural moment. For me, as someone who works in digital editorial and audience engagement for a media manufacturer that covers tech and news, the data is staggering. It also reminds me of when I stumbled into the Grand Theft Auto universe in my twenties. In 2009, I was fresh out of Tisch School of the Arts at Newly introduced York University and was auditioning endlessly. I spent my days at castings surrounded by dozens of other girls who looked like me, only prettier. I spent my nights waitressing until the wee hours of the morning, or haphazardly attending parties and clubs where I admittedly hoped to be discovered. These were chaotic times: years of small successes, like a role on Law & Order or a bit part on a soap opera, separated by months upon months of fruitless auditions and absolutely no work. So when a friend from high school reached out to me about a gig recording voice-over for The Ballad of Gay Tony, a 2009 expansion of Grand Theft Auto IV, I swiftly accepted without asking many questions or seeing the script. To be frank, I wouldn’t have known what to ask about how the character interacted with the universe of GTA. My parents were strict, especially about video games. They were both educators and categorized video games as brain rot before that was even a thing, so I’d never played GTA before. I recorded Joni’s voice track in a couple of hours at Rockstar Games in SoHo, with my high school friend in the audio booth. This was the easiest acting job—there hadn’t been any awkward audition, all of my scenes were set in a nightclub, which was an environment I knew well, and I didn’t have to memorize anything. I just had a sheet of one-liners to deliver in a sassy club manager voice. Since I was a waitress at the time, I remember using one of my managers from The Coffee Shop on Union Square as inspiration. (I won’t name her out of respect.) [Screenshot: Rockstar Games] I needed to separate the character from myself because I wasn’t half as bold as Joni, who spent a lot of time propositioning Luis while simultaneously mocking his, er, body part size. It seems crucial to note that I didn’t realize players could interact with characters beyond speaking to them—in ways that are both violent and sexually violent—but I’m not sure I would’ve turned down the job even if I had known. After all, Joni was a character, she was just an avatar, and I was an actress. I left the studio with few regrets, and even fewer when the check cleared on time. This was 2009. The term “digital footprint” wasn’t part of the zeitgeist. Instagram didn’t exist, and I still typed websites I liked into my browser to check the news—and none of those sites covered gamer culture. Could I have anticipated that Grand Theft Auto would remain a cultural phenomenon that would follow me forever? I don’t think so. I also didn’t run in circles where “fandoms” were a thing, so I was surprised when fans of Joni started emailing me in 2010. In hindsight, this speaks to the growing popularity of the GTA franchise, and the fact that Joni was probably a lot of people’s cup of tea. Their emails were typically short and bizarre, and a few were desperate for a response. It takes a lot of deep thinking about a character to research the voice-over actor and email her, but if there’s one skill I already possessed at age 26, it was knowing that often no response is the best response. Not long after I recorded my voice-over for GTA, I began to suspect I had skills beyond acting. Motivated by the fact that I never felt particularly intrigued by the scripts I was given to audition for, I created my own web series, took a job managing social media and, through a combination of hard work and luck, very quickly built a media career. In 2011 or 2012, I took my acting website down and the emails stopped. When Instagram introduced direct messages, the messages returned, but at a slower pace. During the pandemic, I managed an editorial team that included a section dedicated to gaming. I’d all but forgotten about Joni, but decided to trot out my voice-over credit as a fun fact during one of those team meetings where we were all trying to bond as humans while working from home in isolation. When we finally returned to the office, one of the producers who’d been on the call brought me a poster of Joni as a gift. I unrolled it at my desk. There she was, a reminder of a period in my life when any job that was even moderately creative seemed preferable to serving mojitos. On the poster, Joni is happy as can be, spraying champagne into the air and grinning in her pink dress. It dawned on me that some of the people on my team had been teenagers when the game came out. I thanked the producer and tried not to imagine what sorts of interactions he might have had with Joni. I’ve managed to scrub much of my twenties from the internet—a feat I suspect only elder millennials will be able to pull off, as the internet grows more permanent and everyone becomes increasingly obsessed with saving “receipts.” But Joni is still out there. She occasionally resurfaces in my professional life, partly because Rockstar Games remains a cultural force, and partly because the way players interact with characters—especially women—is still a conversation worth having. I’ve spent years putting distance between myself and the person I was when I voiced her. Joni, meanwhile, is still in that pink dress, spraying champagne, having the time of her life.

#11758. Affordable AI takes more than a lower price
