📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Affordable AI takes more than a lower price

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that elizabeth Field DiGiovanni runs Parcel Air, which makes travel activity boxes designed to keep young children occupied on flights.
  • Elizabeth Field DiGiovanni runs Parcel Air, which makes travel activity boxes designed to keep young children occupied on flights.
  • In a recent development, she was sourcing—finding factories that could make what she needed and getting the job quoted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that elizabeth Field DiGiovanni runs Parcel Air, which makes travel activity boxes designed to keep young children occupied on flights. Everything that goes into the Los Angeles solopreneur’s boxes has to come from somewhere: the toys, the crayons, the packaging. Most of the factories she works with are in Asia, where the workday begins around the time Elizabeth is putting her 4-year-old and her 2-year-old to bed. She was sourcing—finding factories that could make what she needed and getting the job quoted. Those questions run in sequence; each answer sets up the next. A minimum order quantity changes which price break to ask about. A certification answer decides whether lead time matters at all. With the time difference, every link in that chain cost her a day. One vendor negotiation took more than three weeks to produce a quote. AI agents for e-commerce could have done that work for her. Elizabeth assumed reaching that point meant a week of setup she could not spare, choosing among tools and connecting her catalog and supplier list. Now one of our customers, Elizabeth told us when discussing a case study that while running a organization she was also minding two small children at home, and there is rarely a free minute. AI AFFORDABILITY Affordability, for a business like hers, includes the total cost of adoption. A Goldman Sachs survey conducted in August found that 86% of surveyed alumni of its 10,000 Small Businesses program were using AI, but only 15% had fully integrated it into their core operations. Those owners completed a business education program, so they generally sit ahead of small firms. Separately, Census Bureau data from December 2025 to May 2026 showed AI use below 20% among U.S. employer businesses with four or fewer employees, compared with 37% among those with at least 250. Meanwhile, Stanford’s 2025 AI Index tracked the cost of querying a model at roughly GPT-3.5-level performance from $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 by October 2024. We have watched the same curve inside our own product, Accio, where token cost fell by half in four months while consumption grew tenfold. Lowering the cost of intelligence still leaves the work required to put it to use. THE COSTS BEYOND THE SUBSCRIPTION Someone still has to configure the tools, understand the business questions, and check the results. Larger companies can spread that work across teams. Parcel Air has no employees, so Elizabeth performs all of it. Those demands belong in any affordability calculation. The companies building these systems, ours included, can lower them at three levels. 1. Lower the technical barrier An owner looking for suppliers should be able to start with that job, without first learning model selection, prompt engineering, or software integration. Without dedicated IT teams, small businesses have little capacity to assemble and maintain AI systems. Pre-configured expert agents and sourcing plugins do that work in advance, reducing the configuration, custom development, and integration an owner would otherwise take on. 2. Close the expertise gap For AI agents for e-commerce to deliver value, they must combine technical simplicity with an understanding of how businesses source, trade, and operate. A tariff changes landed cost. A missing certification can prevent goods from entering a market. Supplier screening and international logistics require knowledge that owners without procurement teams may not have. Developers can embed that knowledge inside the owner’s workflow. Owners should still be able to see what needs checking, with the system flagging missing information and claims requiring documentation. 3. Make autonomy easier to trust An agent that requires constant supervision can create as much work as it removes. Unlimited authority, however, introduces risks an owner may not be able to afford. Owners need clear permissions, a visible record of actions, and the ability to inspect recommendations and intervene. Routine supplier research and organizing quotes can run independently once the workflow is proven. Orders, payments, and contractual commitments should require explicit human approval. Those controls belong in the product itself. The goal is less routine supervision while the owner keeps control over consequential decisions. WHAT CHANGED FOR PARCEL AIR Elizabeth sources through Alibaba.com and runs this work on Accio, our AI agent designed for small businesses and solo founders. She briefs it the way she would brief a colleague. Before bed, she writes out what she needs: the product, her target cost, the safety certifications, and the quantity. The agents work with suppliers through the business day in Asia while she sleeps. In the morning, before the children are up, she reads what came back and makes the call. She described it to us as having an entire APAC team on the night shift. The first time she ran it properly, she claims, the AI went through 68 suppliers in 3 minutes and 17 seconds. A quote that used to take three weeks came back in 12 hours. She still sets the target cost. She still decides which supplier to trust and which certification claim needs a document behind it. What changed was the waiting. She stopped losing a day to every question, and she got her evenings back. MEASURE THE FULL COST OF ADOPTION Those of us who build AI tools for small businesses should be able to answer two questions. How much time does it take an owner to get a useful result, including setup and learning? And how much time does the tool save on recurring tasks once you factor in setup, review, and upkeep? For a small business owner, the real test comes when the tool becomes part of a busy workweek. Small businesses everywhere should be able to afford to put AI to work. As Elizabeth puts it, “You don’t need a bigger team. You need the night shift covered.” Kuo Zhang is president of Global B2B Business at Alibaba Ecommerce Group.

The major takeaway might be that Samsung is looking to launch one of these bezel-less display options within the Galaxy S27 lineup. An early adoption might indicate that even though this supplier planned on developing these displays for an upcoming Galaxy device, Samsung may want to push the timeline forward and fit it to one of the Galaxy S27 series phones.

Odds are it would be the most expensive option’s display that gets updated – the Galaxy S27 Ultra. It’s also possible it could show up on both the Pro and Ultra variants, to stretch the premium tag across the upper end of the lineup.

#11756. Cities built 311—teachers need one, too

Cities built 311—teachers need one, too

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as a 27-year veteran physics teacher, 2011 Connecticut State Teacher of the Year, and 2023 inductee into the national teachers’ hall of fame, Kristen Record knew how to teach.
  • It has been revealed that as a 27-year veteran physics teacher, 2011 Connecticut State Teacher of the Year, and 2023 inductee into the national teachers’ hall of fame, Kristen Record knew how to teach.
  • In a phone interview with this article’s coauthor, Talia Milgrom-Elcott, Record described a student who loved science but whose severe dyslexia made chemistry, with its letters, numbers, and subscripts, a challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as a 27-year veteran physics teacher, 2011 Connecticut State Teacher of the Year, and 2023 inductee into the national teachers’ hall of fame, Kristen Record knew how to teach. But last year, she ran up against the limits of her vast knowledge base when she stepped in to fill a vacancy and teach honors chemistry at her suburban high school in Stratford, CT. In a phone interview with this article’s coauthor, Talia Milgrom-Elcott, Record described a student who loved science but whose severe dyslexia made chemistry, with its letters, numbers, and subscripts, a challenge. Working with his parents and a special education coordinator, Record turned to the internet, YouTube, and AI for answers. She lacked the knowledge and tools to support him on her own, and because none of the other science or special education teachers had any expertise in this area, she had nowhere else to turn. As more AI tools and edtech platforms enter the scene, the marketplace of information teachers turn to for support has become more crowded and confusing, even for those working inside their areas of expertise. The abundance of available tools places the burden on teachers to determine which are effective, for which students, and under what circumstances, often with little guidance or support. LESSONS FROM LOCAL GOVERNMENT AND MEDICINE New York City had a version of this problem. Residents faced more than 40 agency call centers and no clear way to know which to call. In 2003, the city released 311, a single number for every non-emergency question, reachable by phone, text, app, or web. By 2022, it had received at least 500 million contacts, and cities around the world have copied it. Medicine has UpToDate, a clinical reference written and continually updated by more than 7,000 paid physician authors and reviewers. A doctor unsure of how to treat something gets a practical synthesis of the current evidence instead of a stack of raw studies. Both examples point to something education still lacks: a “Teacher 311.” This single go-to source would turn scattered expertise into clear answers that teachers can depend on. Building one would take rethinking and reinvesting in our nation’s education research infrastructure. HOW A TEACHER 311 COULD WORK A Teacher 311 could look like a texting-based hotline crossed with a living research engine. A teacher like Record could text or chat a question: How do I teach symbolic chemistry notation to a student with severe dyslexia? They would get back a specific, vetted answer instead of an unwieldy list of search results. Behind the scenes, master teachers, researchers, and school system leaders—paid for their expertise—would brainstorm suggestions and review AI-generated recommendations. They would set the standards for what the system would draw on: peer-reviewed research and educator-verified practices. Privacy protections would be built in from the start. As quality is proven and trust earned, AI could take on more of the first draft, but an expert would still review every answer. Teachers would rate responses, so the system improves with each question. The best answers to common questions would proactively go out to teacher networks and professional associations nationwide. Questions without ready answers would fuel the pipeline for education R&D those asked most often or with the highest potential impact on students would be prioritized. For years, the Institute of Education Sciences and U.S. Department of Education have been urging researchers to focus on “knowledge mobilization”: closing the gap between what research tells us and what reaches teachers and students. A Teacher 311 could be that bridge. WHAT’S NEEDED TO CREATE TEACHER 311 The idea for Teacher 311 came from Talia, who developed the concept and the plan to build it. Partnering with Alliance for Learning Innovation (ALI) made sense given its work on federal education R&D policy. ALI’s latest policy brief asks the federal government to build that infrastructure—the capacity to research and test ideas like Teacher 311 before they scale, so the ones that reach classrooms actually work. Senators Bennet (D-CO), Tillis (R-NC), and Van Hollen (D-MD) echoed that call in September when they reintroduced the New Essential Education Discoveries (NEED) Act. If passed, the bill would create the kind of agile center that could seed the investment to build and scale a project like Teacher 311. The federal government is well positioned to back something like this, and an administration that did could make it a signature service and a hallmark of its tenure. In the meantime, the private and philanthropic sectors have the opportunity to move the needle now. We estimate that the Teacher 311 hub would cost less than $5 million to build and $3 million per year to run, a fraction of the $2.55 billion the federal government allocated in fiscal year 2022 for education R&D (the year ALI conducted a funding analysis). Done right, the payoff would reach every level of the system. The Institute of Education Sciences and the National Science Foundation would gain a steady, practitioner-driven pipeline of research questions worth funding. States and districts would get better evidence on where to invest in professional learning. Most importantly, teachers would get useful, trusted guidance on the problems they’re facing, and their students would benefit. Teachers search for solutions every day to help their students. Record figured it out eventually, mostly on her own. The next teacher with a student like hers shouldn’t have to. Sara Schapiro is executive director of Alliance for Learning Innovation. Talia Milgrom-Elcott is cofounder and executive director of Beyond100K and Starfish Institute.

#11753. The energy strategy most companies don’t have

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1393 w)

The energy strategy most companies don’t have

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for trucking fleets, manufacturers, and other energy-intensive businesses, energy has been little more than a line item for the past two decades.
  • For trucking fleets, manufacturers, and other energy-intensive businesses, energy has been little more than a line item for the past two decades.
  • Global energy use keeps growing and electricity demand is rising more than twice as fast as energy use overall, according to the International Energy Agency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for trucking fleets, manufacturers, and other energy-intensive businesses, energy has been little more than a line item for the past two decades. Today it’s a competitive variable. Whether a business can secure the energy it needs—and afford it—increasingly determines whether it can grow. Global energy use keeps growing and electricity demand is rising more than twice as fast as energy use overall, according to the International Energy Agency. The problem is that war and geopolitical conflict, along with tariffs reshaping the cost of equipment, are affecting supply and cost. Policies are also shifting with election cycles. This year alone, oil swung from $118 a barrel to under $72 and back above $100, while Washington rewrote the nation’s fuel-economy rules. No single shock is decisive—the shocks compound. As a result, nearly every fleet and fuel-retail operator I speak with is wrestling with whether to use electric, diesel, or natural gas. However, energy markets are moving too fast and too unevenly for anyone to call it with confidence. The operators pulling ahead have stopped trying to choose one. Instead, they’re building the capability of running on more than one energy source—and deciding in real time which to use, where, and when. FedEx is a case in point. It now runs nearly 9,500 electric vehicles while testing renewable diesel for the long-haul trucks where, as the company puts it, “full electrification is not yet feasible at scale.” And it isn’t alone: Roughly 19% of North American fleets now operate EVs, and 30% run hybrid or alternative-fuel vehicles. PAY FOR FLEXIBILITY WHERE IT COUNTS Optionality isn’t free. A second energy source means added infrastructure, more complex procurement and, often, some loss of efficiency. No business can hedge everything. The discipline is deciding where flexibility is worth paying for. The most resilient operators I see ask two questions about every site, route, and asset: If this energy source were disrupted tomorrow, how much revenue would stop? And how exposed is it to a single fuel, supplier, or grid connection? Where both answers are high, redundancy is insurance worth buying now. A delivery depot that charges its entire fleet from one utility feed can’t run routes when that feed goes down. Where impact is high but exposure is modest, flexible supply contracts, rather than long-term agreements locking in a single source, may be enough. Where the impact is low, optimize for cost and move on. THE EASY PART IS THE HARDWARE Adding EV chargers to a forecourt or alternative-fuel trucks to a fleet is now easy. Running them together is not. A mixed-energy operation creates decisions a single-fuel business never faced. Which vehicle takes which route, given its charge level and the day’s energy prices? When should a depot charge its equipment to avoid peak demand costs? How do you compare cost per mile across diesel, natural gas, and electric when the data lives in separate systems? The advantage goes to businesses that can see their entire energy picture in one place and act on it. In a volatile market, the ability to switch is only as valuable as the ability to know when to switch. 3 MOVES WORTH MAKING NOW For leaders of fleet, fuel-retail, and other energy-intensive businesses, building a multi-energy operation starts with understanding where you’re vulnerable and what flexibility is worth. These three moves lay that groundwork. 1. Map your 24-hour exposure. Identify the sites, routes, and assets that would stop generating revenue within a day of losing their primary energy source. 2. Put a price on flexibility. Capital cases that compare only cost per gallon or per kilowatt-hour miss the value of being able to switch. Make the cost of downtime an explicit line in every energy investment. 3. Instrument before you diversify. You can’t coordinate what you can’t see. Bring fuel, charging, payments, and fleet data into a single view before adding the next energy source. Energy isn’t going to get more predictable. Leaders who build for adaptability will succeed whichever way it goes. As an executive, ask yourself: If your primary energy source were disrupted tomorrow, how rapidly could your business respond? Mark Morelli is president and CEO of Vontier.

Industry News: 5 leadership lessons the music industry taught me

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, spend enough time around live music and you rapidly learn that the talent standing in the spotlight is only a small part of what makes a great show.
  • Sources indicate that spend enough time around live music and you swiftly learn that the talent standing in the spotlight is only a small part of what makes a great show.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve spent much of my career working in the music industry, from marketing and business development to managing independent venues and festivals, with stops along the way at Graceland, Fun Fun Fun Fest, DoStuff Media, and SXSW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, spend enough time around live music and you rapidly learn that the talent standing in the spotlight is only a small part of what makes a great show. Behind every successful performance is an entire team of talented people working together to make awesome moments happen. I’ve spent much of my career working in the music industry, from marketing and business development to managing independent venues and festivals, with stops along the way at Graceland, Fun Fun Fun Fest, DoStuff Media, and SXSW. I’ve also spent plenty of time playing music myself, including a period when I was pretty convinced I’d be the next Dave Matthews. Today, as Huntsville, Alabama’s Music Officer, I’ve found that many lessons I learned working with artists, agents, promoters, production teams, business executives, interns, and others have been just as valuable in government as in the music business. Here are five leadership lessons the music industry taught me that apply to most professions. 1. IF YOU SAY YOU’RE GOING TO DO SOMETHING, DO IT. Reliability is a highly underrated leadership quality. One of the quickest ways to lose your team’s confidence is surprisingly simple: Tell someone you’re going to do something and then don’t follow through. The lead guitarist might have incredible talent, but if they’re consistently late and unprepared, the band probably won’t be enthusiastic about working with them. Whether it’s finishing a project, making an introduction, or getting someone the information they need to move forward, people rely on those commitments. Not delivering on responsibilities can throw everything off course. Trust is ultimately built through what’s delivered. 2. YOU DON’T NEED TO BE THE SMARTEST PERSON IN THE ROOM. Nobody has all the answers, and being in a leadership position doesn’t automatically make your ideas the best ones. Some of the most creative and effective solutions I’ve encountered came from people closest to the work. Think about everything involved in producing a concert. The sound engineer understands things about audio the promoter probably doesn’t. The lighting director has perfected their craft. The artist, stage manager, marketing team, and venue operators have their own areas of expertise. How much harder would that operation be if everyone had to defer to one person who believed they knew more than everybody else? Create an environment where people feel valued and empowered to speak up, challenge ideas, and suggest better ways of doing things. 3. SOMETIMES THE BEST LEADERS GET OUT OF THE WAY. Musicians, technicians, stagehands, managers, security staff, and ticket sellers have specific responsibilities. When everyone knows what they’re doing, the operation runs so smoothly that most in the audience don’t think about the work happening behind the scenes. Sometimes a well-intentioned person jumping in to “help” can make things harder. The same applies to leadership. If you’ve assembled a great team, trust people to do their jobs. Your team should know you’re there when they need resources or guidance, but there’s a fine line between supporting and micromanaging. 4. BE A CHAMELEON WITHOUT BEING FAKE. In music, I worked with artists, business executives, concert promoters, venue operators, and community organizations. In government, I’ve added elected officials, city departments, and other stakeholders to that mix. Each group has its own priorities and communication styles. Learn how to adapt to those environments without compromising who you are. Understand the room you’re walking into. What matters to and motivates the people you’re talking with? What do they need to understand to make a decision? There’s a distinction between adapting your communication and claiming expertise you don’t have. Don’t change your values based on who’s in the room and don’t underestimate how quickly talented, experienced people can recognize when someone isn’t being genuine. 5. EARN THE RIGHT TO TAKE BIGGER SWINGS. Making the transition into local government from a music industry career came with culture shock. The music business naturally rewards creativity, experimentation, and taking risks. Government, for good reason, places greater emphasis on process, accountability, and responsibly allocating public resources. Those two approaches don’t have to be mutually exclusive. Some of the most meaningful progress happens when you bring an entrepreneurial mindset into an environment not accustomed to doing things differently. The key is understanding that you must earn the trust to experiment. Plenty of people seem more interested in being viewed as innovative rather than doing the work necessary to make their ideas successful. Making a bold move to prove you’re a bold leader isn’t a good strategy. Instead, focus on building credibility through consistent execution, responsible decisions, and a track record of delivering results. Trust is organizational capital. When you follow through on a commitment, solve a problem, or demonstrate sound judgment, you build more of it. Eventually, that credibility allows you to propose bigger ideas and challenge conventional thinking. These calculated risks might otherwise struggle to gain support. When you do take big swings, be thoughtful about potential consequences. Make sure the people involved understand the vision, the risks, and what you’re trying to accomplish. The goal should be to build something meaningful that creates opportunities and continues delivering value years down the road. LEADERS: IT’S NOT ALL ABOUT YOU The most vital things I’ve learned about leadership came from working alongside talented people who knew how to get things done under pressure, and without much recognition. The best live performances are successful because people understand their roles, trust one another, communicate effectively, and take pride in contributing to something bigger than themselves. The same is true of great organizations. While the headliner gets applause, the entire team makes the show possible. Great leaders make sure everyone gets a standing ovation. Matt Mandrella is music officer of the City of Huntsville.

Sources indicate that spend enough time around live music and you swiftly learn that the talent standing in the spotlight is only a small part of what makes a great show. Behind every successful performance is an entire team of talented people working together to make awesome moments happen.

According to recent reports, I’ve spent much of my career working in the music industry, from marketing and business development to managing independent venues and festivals, with stops along the way at Graceland, Fun Fun Fun Fest, DoStuff Media, and SXSW. I’ve also spent plenty of time playing music myself, including a period when I was pretty convinced I’d be the next Dave Matthews.

Today, as Huntsville, Alabama’s Music Officer, I’ve found that many lessons I learned working with artists, agents, promoters, production teams, business executives, interns, and others have been just as valuable in government as in the music business.

Here are five leadership lessons the music industry taught me that apply to most professions.

Industry observers note that reliability is a highly underrated leadership quality. One of the quickest ways to lose your team’s confidence is surprisingly simple: Tell someone you’re going to do something and then don’t follow through.

The lead guitarist might have incredible talent, but if they’re consistently late and unprepared, the band probably won’t be enthusiastic about working with them.

Sources indicate that whether it’s finishing a project, making an introduction, or getting someone the information they need to move forward, people rely on those commitments. Not delivering on responsibilities can throw everything off course. Trust is ultimately built through what’s delivered.

Nobody has all the answers, and being in a leadership position doesn’t automatically make your ideas the best ones. Some of the most creative and effective solutions I’ve encountered came from people closest to the work.

Think about everything involved in producing a concert. The sound engineer understands things about audio the promoter probably doesn’t. The lighting director has perfected their craft. The artist, stage manager, marketing team, and venue operators have their own areas of expertise. How much harder would that operation be if everyone had to defer to one person who believed they knew more than everybody else?

Create an environment where people feel valued and empowered to speak up, challenge ideas, and suggest better ways of doing things.

Musicians, technicians, stagehands, managers, security staff, and ticket sellers have specific responsibilities. When everyone knows what they’re doing, the operation runs so smoothly that most in the audience don’t think about the work happening behind the scenes.

Sometimes a well-intentioned person jumping in to “help” can make things harder. The same applies to leadership. If you’ve assembled a great team, trust people to do their jobs. Your team should know you’re there when they need resources or guidance, but there’s a fine line between supporting and micromanaging.

In music, I worked with artists, business executives, concert promoters, venue operators, and community organizations. In government, I’ve added elected officials, city departments, and other stakeholders to that mix.

Each group has its own priorities and communication styles. Learn how to adapt to those environments without compromising who you are. Understand the room you’re walking into. What matters to and motivates the people you’re talking with? What do they need to understand to make a decision?

Recent findings suggest that there’s a distinction between adapting your communication and claiming expertise you don’t have. Don’t change your values based on who’s in the room and don’t underestimate how swiftly talented, experienced people can recognize when someone isn’t being genuine.

Industry observers note that making the transition into local government from a music industry career came with culture shock. The music business naturally rewards creativity, experimentation, and taking risks. Government, for good reason, places greater emphasis on process, accountability, and responsibly allocating public resources.

Those two approaches don’t have to be mutually exclusive. Some of the most meaningful progress happens when you bring an entrepreneurial mindset into an environment not accustomed to doing things differently. The key is understanding that you must earn the trust to experiment.

Plenty of people seem more interested in being viewed as innovative rather than doing the work necessary to make their ideas successful. Making a bold move to prove you’re a bold leader isn’t a good strategy. Instead, focus on building credibility through consistent execution, responsible decisions, and a track record of delivering results.

Trust is organizational capital. When you follow through on a commitment, solve a problem, or demonstrate sound judgment, you build more of it. Eventually, that credibility allows you to propose bigger ideas and challenge conventional thinking. These calculated risks might otherwise struggle to gain support.

When you do take substantial swings, be thoughtful about potential consequences. Make sure the people involved understand the vision, the risks, and what you’re trying to accomplish. The goal should be to build something meaningful that creates opportunities and continues delivering value years down the road.

The most vital things I’ve learned about leadership came from working alongside talented people who knew how to get things done under pressure, and without much recognition.

Sources indicate that the best live performances are successful because people understand their roles, trust one another, communicate effectively, and take pride in contributing to something bigger than themselves. The same is true of great organizations.

Recent findings suggest that while the headliner gets applause, the entire team makes the show possible. Great leaders make sure everyone gets a standing ovation.

Matt Mandrella is music officer of the City of Huntsville.

#11751. You can now Email and Text (via Google Messages, iMessage) with Gemini

You can now Email and Text (via Google Messages, iMessage) with Gemini

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.
  • According to recent reports, instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication.
  • You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.

According to recent reports, instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication. To get started, go to gemini.google.com/channels.

You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries.

In a recent development, text with Gemini works via Google Messages and iMessage. Google does note that this method is “not end-to-end encrypted and may be accessible by your carrier.” The setup process involves verifying a phone number. Existing numbers associated with your Google Account appear automatically, and there’s the ability to add a newly introduced one.

Afterward, you’ll receive a text from Gemini via RCS Business Messaging that offers a pretty straightforward chat experience. Before sending, booking, or other “major actions,” Gemini will ask for 1-tap confirmation.

Recent findings suggest that …you can text a request, snap a photo of a school flyer to add dates to your Google Calendar, or get scheduled check-ins in a private 1:1 thread. If your plans change while Gemini is working, simply reply to the text to steer the task mid-run without starting over.

(Amusingly, Text with Gemini coexists with the existing Google Messages integration, which you can distinguish by the old blue/purple icon.).

In a recent development, email with Gemini lets you “start tasks and get updates by emailing” gemini@google.com. Google explicitly names Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook as supported clients, while emails from Gemini are always “1:1 to you (never “Reply-All”) with a link to review and confirm your results.”.

Forward a batch of school emails to add key dates to Google Calendar, spot schedule conflicts, or send over threads and PDFs to sort out medical bills and track insurance renewals.

It has been revealed that you can manage phone numbers and turn off both options from this latest Channels page. If you’re more familiar with using your email client or phone’s messaging app, Text and Email with Gemini might boost your assistant usage. This is available first in the US.

Meanwhile, when unveiled in May, these two options were intended for Gemini Spark, which has since been integrated into the main Gemini experience as “tasks.”.

#11749. 22 leadership insights on ensuring accountability without instilling fear

22 leadership insights on ensuring accountability without instilling fear

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix.
  • In a recent development, accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix.
  • Sources indicate that we asked members of the Fast Manufacturer Impact Council how they ensure accountability without creating fear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that accountability has always been crucial, and more so now that artificial intelligence is in the mix. The term can come with negative connotations: If something goes wrong, it means whoever is accountable is to blame. Fearing accountability, some team members may hesitate to take roles that require much of it. Even if they step up, fear can keep them from doing their best work or taking needed risks. We asked members of the Fast Organization Impact Council how they ensure accountability without creating fear. Below, 22 of them share their best advice on keeping accountability as a necessary and positive role instead of something people dread. 1. TREAT MISSES AS INFORMATION Be as clear about expectations up front as you are about results afterward. Fear comes from ambiguity: People don’t know what success looks like until they’ve missed it. I set clear owners and outcomes at the start, then treat misses as information. What did we learn, and what do we change? I also name my own misses out loud, before anyone else’s. When the leader models it, accountability stops feeling like judgment and becomes a shared standard the whole team owns. — Megan Noel, Covista 2. MODEL SELF-REFLECTION Accountability is less likely to create fear when leaders hold themselves accountable to the same standards and deadlines they expect of others, are honest about where they fell short, and share the lessons they learned. The more leaders model that kind of self-reflection, the more comfortable others will feel doing the same—and helping their teammates build that skill. — Grace Keith Rodriguez, Caliber Corporate Advisers 3. FOCUS ON LESSONS LEARNED Accountability should give people the confidence to take major swings. When it only shows up for the misses and mistakes, you create a culture of fear, which doesn’t inspire creativity or big thinking. Instead, be clear about expectations, set ambitious goals together, and when something falls short, focus on the lesson learned and move on. — Max Friedman, Givebutter 4. LEAD WITH CURIOSITY RATHER THAN BLAME Accountability without fear begins with clarity—clear expectations and realistic goals—balanced with my personal commitment to being accessible and providing timely feedback. This shared accountability builds trust as the same standards apply at both levels. When challenges arise, I am able to lead with curiosity rather than blame, asking “What happened, and what support do you need?” which creates space for my team to surface problems early and treat setbacks as learning opportunities. Consistency reinforces this sense of safety, so instead of fearing accountability, my team feels supported and invested in our shared success. — Maurice Twomey, Roto 5. ENSURE REAL ALIGNMENT FROM THE START Many tend to think of accountability as something you create at the end of a process. Someone didn’t do what they were supposed to do. Will you hold them accountable or not? In my experience, however, accountability issues are often alignment issues in disguise. What are we trying to do and why? By when? What are we both assuming? What is really feasible? Good leaders ensure there is real alignment around these questions at the start of a process. They approach accountability not as a punishment question but as a clarity question—and in doing so, they debunk the idea that accountability and fear must come hand-in-hand. — Maril MacDonald, Gagen MacDonald 6. OWN THE OUTDATED DASHBOARD Accountability isn’t perfection. A team member flagged outdated targets on a dashboard I was presenting. I owned it and thanked them. Small moments like that set the tone for the big ones. When we miss a real target, we own our work and our choices and solve it as a team. Do that consistently, and you build that muscle for the harder moments. — Michele Walsh, UNICEF USA 7. SHIFT THE MINDSET When leaders shift their mindset from “don’t break this” to “let’s try this,” accountability becomes about outcomes and learning. As leaders, we need to role model what strong accountability looks like and acknowledge fear with grace and empathy. This means we should understand that some good ideas won’t stick, and we should celebrate innovative thinking even when it doesn’t result in a win. When people see their leader take a smart risk, own what follows, and adapt quickly, they do the same. — Jacqui Canney, ServiceNow 8. CUT THE ENDLESS APPROVAL CHAINS If you want real accountability, let team members own the outcome and cut the endless approval chains. Nobody likes to fail, but you can build a culture of permissible failure and actually walk the talk. When mistakes happen, address them head-on, take the lesson, and move on fast. — Khozema Shipchandler, Twilio 9. ASK WHAT HAPPENED, NOT WHO DID IT Make the destination crystal clear and the path flexible. Fear shows up when people don’t know what “good” looks like until they miss it. I’d rather over-communicate the outcome, agree on ownership out loud, and let people choose how they get there. When something goes sideways, my first question is “What happened?” not “Who did this?” Accountability is a promise teammates make to each other, not a punishment waiting to happen. — Colby Proffitt, Seekr 10. MAKE ACCOUNTABILITY A WEEKLY RHYTHM Accountability works when colleagues do the flagging, not the leader. Every week, especially in our executive meetings, we review our trackers top to bottom and call out anything blocked or at risk, in the open, in front of the team. It’s rare that someone gets blindsided in a one-on-one weeks later. Fear creeps in when accountability feels personal or arbitrary. A visible, weekly rhythm makes it structural instead, and that is what keeps people honest without making them defensive. Consistent communication is key. Beyond email and Slack, good ole phone calls and texts are quite effective. — Cody Barbo, Trust & Will 11. TEACH CLEAN ESCALATION For our team, it all starts with providing clear communication so people understand what’s expected and how success will be measured. We approach conversations from a point of kindness and empathy, which includes listening and practicing radical candor so everyone is provided honest, respectful feedback and knows where they stand. Teaching clean escalation and other techniques also plays a role in maximizing accountability while preserving the best possible team dynamics. When people know they can raise issues early and get help addressing them, taking responsibility becomes much easier. — Leerom Segal, Klick Health 12. DON’T LEAVE PEOPLE GUESSING Clarity, transparency, and continuous communication. That is the foundation—and frankly, it is the ethos on which we built our company. When people know exactly what is expected, where they stand, and that honest feedback flows early and often, there is nothing to fear. Fear creeps in when people are left guessing. The goal is shared accountability. Not imposed from the top down but owned collectively by a team that feels genuinely empowered. When that culture exists, people hold each other to a higher standard because they want to—not because they have to. — Meredith Rosenberg, NU Advisory Partners 13. THE KIND OF FEAR MATTERS Fear isn’t always bad. Fearing your boss is different from fearing you didn’t do your best work. Top-down fear can produce compliance, but rarely excellence. I want my team accountable to themselves first, because people only do their best work on things they care about. That means clear quarterly and annual goals, professional development funds for growth areas, honest conversations about where they want to go, and a real grasp of why our work matters and why their contribution is key. People who hold themselves to a standard outperform people who only answer to a boss. — Muneer Panjwani, Engage for Good | The Halo Awards 14. ATTACH A HUMAN OWNER TO AI-RELATED DECISIONS I would argue that it is the lack of accountability that creates fear. Accountability should remove ambiguity. Each artificial intelligence-related decision should have a human owner. There are clear rules of engagement that establish what is and is not in the bounds of permissibility. And when mistakes are made, they are inspected and not concealed. Fear breeds in darkness: Create light. — Scott Brighton, Bonterra 15. HAVE EMPLOYEES SET THE BAR FOR THEMSELVES Accountability is a matter of doing what you commit to. Our team members have some flexibility to set expectations regarding the timing and scope of their deliveries. Publicly demonstrating finished products in team or client meetings improves accountability. Fear is effectively removed when trying to clear bars we set for ourselves. — Brad Weber, InspiringApps 16. SHOW VULNERABILITY Model that it’s ok to own up to a mistake. We’re only human and no one is perfect. Ultimately that leads to greater accountability because there is an honesty at the heart of it. It removes the bullshit and gives folks the support they need to own their accomplishments, warts and all. — Helen Andrews, Johannes Leonardo 17. SET CLEAR EXPECTATIONS Every employee plays a role in the company’s overall success, but depending on their level or access to senior leadership, they may not see how their contributions impact the greater whole. What is important to the CEO? What are the growth ambitions of the company? How does each individual’s responsibilities ladder up to the organization’s goals? It is essential to set clear expectations for each person, provide honest feedback, and communicate transparently about how daily activities and individual performance are linked to company success. — Celia Jones, FINN Partners 18. WRITE IT DOWN Accountability holds when the measure is agreed before the work starts. Clarity is kindness, as they say. Set it together, write it down, and review it on a fixed schedule so a missed target shows up early and gets treated as information. People get defensive when the standard appears after the result, or when it shifts depending on who’s asking. Other than that, I try to give real guidelines and real feedback. If you start off that way, it instills the proper expectation of communication. — James Chester, WVN 19. DISCUSS HOW TO CLOSE THE PERFORMANCE-EXPECTATION GAP I try to set a high bar of excellence by sharing great work, and by praising and rewarding excellent work. That way, when someone isn’t delivering, we can point to the gap between their performance and the expectation and talk about how to close the gap. It’s designed to create a supportive, safe, and fair environment. No finger pointing and passive-aggressiveness allowed! — Phillip Haid, Public Inc. 20. TAKE AN ASPIRATIONAL APPROACH I’ve learned that empathy and accountability aren’t opposites. A few years ago, I leaned too far into being accommodating, and expectations slipped. I used to frame performance gaps as “We’re not where we need to be,” which I think created fear. Through coaching, I learned to take a more aspirational approach: “This is what excellence looks like. How can we get there?” It shifts the focus from fear to problem-solving. When people care deeply about the mission and understand what’s expected of them, accountability becomes a shared responsibility rather than something driven by fear. — Felicia Curcuru, Binti 21. REPLACE PUNITIVE REACTIONS WITH CURIOSITY AND COLLABORATION Having experienced the damage of fear-based leadership early in my career, I know criticism and punishment only breed toxicity and burnout. Accountability without fear starts with connecting our work to purpose. At a mission-based organization, holding ourselves accountable is directly tied to achieving our mission. When performance issues arise, leaders should replace punitive reactions with curiosity and collaboration. Approaching staff with two-way dialogue to uncover blockers, rather than one-way scrutiny, turns accountability into a partnership that helps everyone succeed. — Jaymes Black, The Trevor Project 22. SEPARATE THE PERSON FROM THE OUTCOME Accountability works best when expectations are clear before something goes wrong. I try to separate the person from the outcome, so the conversation becomes about what happened, what we learned, and what needs to change. Fear makes people hide problems. Clarity makes them easier to solve. — George Kailas, Prospero.ai.

There are clear rules of engagement that establish what is and is not in the bounds of permissibility. And when mistakes are made, they are inspected and not concealed. Fear breeds in darkness: Create light. — Scott Brighton, Bonterra.

Sources indicate that accountability is a matter of doing what you commit to. Our team members have some flexibility to set expectations regarding the timing and scope of their deliveries. Publicly demonstrating finished products in team or client meetings improves accountability. Fear is effectively removed when trying to clear bars we set for ourselves. — Brad Weber, InspiringApps.

Model that it’s ok to own up to a mistake. We’re only human and no one is perfect. Ultimately that leads to greater accountability because there is an honesty at the heart of it. It removes the bullshit and gives folks the support they need to own their accomplishments, warts and all. — Helen Andrews, Johannes Leonardo.

Every employee plays a role in the tech giant’s overall success, but depending on their level or access to senior leadership, they may not see how their contributions impact the greater whole. What is key to the CEO? What are the growth ambitions of the company? How does each individual’s responsibilities ladder up to the organization’s goals? It is essential to set clear expectations for each person, provide honest feedback, and communicate transparently about how daily activities and individual performance are linked to company success. — Celia Jones, FINN Partners.

Accountability holds when the measure is agreed before the work starts. Clarity is kindness, as they say. Set it together, write it down, and review it on a fixed schedule so a missed target shows up early and gets treated as information. People get defensive when the standard appears after the result, or when it shifts depending on who’s asking. Other than that, I try to give real guidelines and real feedback. If you start off that way, it instills the proper expectation of communication. — James Chester, WVN.

In a recent development, I try to set a high bar of excellence by sharing great work, and by praising and rewarding excellent work. That way, when someone isn’t delivering, we can point to the gap between their performance and the expectation and talk about how to close the gap. It’s designed to create a supportive, safe, and fair environment. No finger pointing and passive-aggressiveness allowed! — Phillip Haid, Public Inc.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve learned that empathy and accountability aren’t opposites. A few years ago, I leaned too far into being accommodating, and expectations slipped. I used to frame performance gaps as “We’re not where we need to be,” which I think created fear. Through coaching, I learned to take a more aspirational approach: “This is what excellence looks like. How can we get there?” It shifts the focus from fear to problem-solving. When people care deeply about the mission and understand what’s expected of them, accountability becomes a shared responsibility rather than something driven by fear. — Felicia Curcuru, Binti.

Industry observers note that having experienced the damage of fear-based leadership early in my career, I know criticism and punishment only breed toxicity and burnout. Accountability without fear starts with connecting our work to purpose. At a mission-based organization, holding ourselves accountable is directly tied to achieving our mission. When performance problems arise, leaders should replace punitive reactions with curiosity and collaboration. Approaching staff with two-way dialogue to uncover blockers, rather than one-way scrutiny, turns accountability into a partnership that helps everyone succeed. — Jaymes Black, The Trevor Project.

Sources indicate that accountability works best when expectations are clear before something goes wrong. I try to separate the person from the outcome, so the conversation becomes about what happened, what we learned, and what needs to change. Fear makes people hide problems. Clarity makes them easier to solve. — George Kailas, Prospero.ai.

Tech Report: Anthropic stock is already falling today: Why AI giants are seeing a painful sell-off after record IPO

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite Anthropic’s (Nasdaq: ANT) blockbuster IPO yesterday, it’s been a bad several weeks for AI-related stocks.
  • Despite Anthropic’s (Nasdaq: ANT) blockbuster IPO yesterday, it’s been a bad several weeks for AI-related stocks.
  • Industry observers note that and today things are even worse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite Anthropic’s (Nasdaq: ANT) blockbuster IPO yesterday, it’s been a bad several weeks for AI-related stocks. And today things are even worse. Nearly every major hardware manufacturer that makes components for the AI pipeline—from CPUs to GPUs to memory—is seeing significant share price declines. And then there’s Anthropic itself, the world’s most valuable pure-play AI firm. After a strong debut yesterday, its share price is down significantly this morning. Here’s what you need to know. What’s happening? In premarket trading this morning, the tech-heavy Nasdaq is seeing red, along with some of the largest AI players that trade there. As of this writing, Nasdaq futures are down nearly 1%. That’s after a significant fall of more than 550 points, or 2.25% yesterday. As of Thursday’s close, the Nasdaq was down around 5% for the week. Yesterday’s Nasdaq drop is all the more striking because it was also the day that Anthropic made its eagerly awaited market debut. The AI company’s IPO was priced at $83 per share, but those shares quickly popped to nearly $115 in early trading before ending the first day at $97.17—a 17% gain. Anthropic’s IPO was the largest in history, raising around $81.3 billion. The company’s market cap now sits at around $1.27 billion, making it the 12th most valuable company on the planet. Yet Anthropic’s success did little for the rest of the market. Throughout the day, tech stocks started falling, including those of other major AI players like Nvidia. This morning, Asian markets and major AI and tech players are down significantly. And on this side of the Pacific, the sell-off is continuing with major American AI-related stocks. As of the time of this writing, the following AI-adjacent stocks are down in premarket:  Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMD): down 6.5% NVIDIA Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA): down 2.3% Intel Corporation (Nasdaq: INTC): down 5.2% Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU): down 4.8% SanDisk Corporation (Nasdaq: SNDK): down 6.7% And yes, Anthropic’s stock price is down nearly 10%. Why are Anthropic’s shares sinking? Anthropic and hardware-related AI companies are both seeing their share prices sink in premarket trading, but maybe for different reasons. When it comes to AI hardware companies, those that make the components needed to power the massive server farms AI data centers require, there has been significant negative sentiment around them since at least October. Investors are increasingly getting uneasy with the major hyperscalers’ capex spending. Companies like Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions to build out data centers, and most aren’t yet showing a clear path to monetizing AI enough to recoup those costs. If those companies cave to investor pressure and start scaling back their capex plans, it will hit AI hardware component makers (like Nvidia, Intel, and AMD) and memory makers (like Micron and SanDisk) pretty hard. Investors seem to be bracing for an inevitable capex pullback, which has weighed heavily on hardware-adjacent AI stocks recently. Other factors that have affected AI stocks lately include the Jensen Huang scandal and the ongoing fears that we are firmly in an AI bubble. But Anthropic doesn’t make hardware, and it just had its successful IPO only yesterday—so why are its shares down so much today? It likely has less to do with significant fears of capex spending and more to do with other factors. The primary factor is likely profit-taking. The company’s stock price rose more than 17% on its first day of trading. Many shareholders who aren’t bound by lockup periods are likely taking some of those profits this morning. Another factor—and one that could have significantly more long-term consequences—is that fears of an AI bubble and an AI slowdown are also likely weighing on investors’ minds. Anthropic has a massive valuation north of $1.2 trillion, but in the first nine months of 2026, the company generated only around $33 billion in revenue. Its net loss for the same period was $104 billion. Investors may be able to live with that discrepancy while the AI hype train is riding high, but enthusiasm only goes so far, and if the AI bubble bursts, Anthropic could be hit hard. Where do Anthropic shares go from here? That’s something everyone wants to know, and no one can tell you. The company’s share price has already fallen from its intraday debut high of nearly $115 per share to its current premarket price of $88.44. Contrast that with the company Anthropic just dethroned as having the largest IPO in history: SpaceX. When SpaceX (Nasdaq: SPCX) went public in June, it was, until yesterday, the biggest IPO in history, raising $75 billion. Its IPO price was $135 per share, and the stock quickly jumped to more than $225 per share. But then it began falling. A month after its debut, SPCX shares were trading below their $135 IPO price as the hype wore off, and people began questioning the company’s future profitability. As of the time of this writing, SPCX shares are trading at just $131.66 in premarket trading. If ANT’s early life plays out the same way—and there’s no way to predict whether it will or won’t—the share price could be underwater for even IPO investors in just a few months. And if the AI bubble does burst, things could get even worse.

Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small upgrade to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history.

According to recent reports, like in the Gemini app, anything you discuss in a temporary thread isn’t saved to your account. It won’t appear in conversation history or influence future recommendations.

These AI Mode responses won’t be personalized with past preferences. After you close a temporary thread, there’s no way to access it again.

Industry observers note that to launch, tap the new pen button with a dotted border in the top-right corner, which is the same icon used in the Gemini app. The personalized greeting at the top of the prompt box switches to “Welcome, stranger.”.

According to recent reports, this is an alternative to opening google.com in Incognito Mode, while still being able to use the model picker. Meanwhile, Google’s use of “threads” to describe AI Mode conversations versus “chats” in the Gemini app is interesting.

Temporary threads are rolling out globally starting today on mobile and desktop browsers across all AI Mode languages.

This joins other changes that Google is still testing for AI Mode. With the latest Google app beta on Android, you can now swiftly upload from Google Drive, which joins Gallery, Camera, and Files as attachment options. You can also now access Canvas on Android.

In a recent development, FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Texas Democrats’ sweeping victory could spell trouble for Elon Musk’s business empire

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that hundreds of millions of dollars later, Elon Musk has some regrets.
  • Hundreds of millions of dollars later, Elon Musk has some regrets.
  • “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” the world’s richest man noted at The New York Times DealBook conference this week, reflecting on the heaps of dollars he poured into Republican campaigns nationwide during this year’s midterm elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hundreds of millions of dollars later, Elon Musk has some regrets. “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” the world’s richest man mentioned at The Upcoming York Times DealBook conference this week, reflecting on the heaps of dollars he poured into Republican campaigns nationwide during this year’s midterm elections. It’s easy to see why he feels that way, particularly in Texas, where Musk has moved his business operations and cultivated close ties with Republican leadership. Despite his extraordinary spending—$446 million, roughly half of which went to races in Texas—Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress and swept the major statewide elections. That eye-popping figure includes $5 million for Republican incumbent Greg Abbott’s gubernatorial campaign and $10 million for Attorney General Ken Paxton’s U.S. Senate bid, both of which ended in defeat. But Musk may soon have much bigger financial headaches than any futile campaign contributions. The incoming Democratic administration in Austin could complicate the billionaire’s plans to expand his sprawling business empire. Indeed, Texas’s governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, has already signaled that she intends to be less accommodating of the kinds of tax breaks and land deals that helped lure Musk to the Lone Star State in the first place. Abbott has by contrast been an enthusiastic champion of Musk’s Texas vision, appearing alongside him at firm events and celebrating his investments in the state. Abbott and Musk reportedly keep in close contact, and the governor’s office even fought to prevent the release of months of communications with the tech mogul’s companies, arguing that they contain “information that is intimate and embarrassing and not of legitimate concern to the public.” With Hinojosa in office, Musk can no longer count on that same level of intimacy, though he did offer a more sanguine assessment of his future in a blue Texas at the DealBook conference, predicting that Hinojosa would govern as a moderate. “I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor,” he said. Billions in tax breaks Musk’s companies have to date been given the royal treatment from the state. SpaceX, for instance, scored roughly $1.66 billion in potential property tax breaks for its planned Terafab semiconductor facility in Grimes County, between College Station and Houston, according to the Houston Chronicle. The incentives, approved by two local school districts under Texas’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation program, could cut the company’s school property taxes in half for 10 years per phase of construction. SpaceX also secured a $30 million grant from the Texas Enterprise Fund. Hinojosa has made no secret of her disdain for such arrangements. “I do think we should wipe clean corporate welfare in this state,” she told the Texas Standard in October, singling out Musk’s billion-dollar-plus tax break. She’s also pushing to reveal to the public more about Musk’s relationship with Abbott. In October, she sued Abbott for access to unredacted emails involving Musk and his companies. But Hinojosa won’t have an easy time undoing those incentives. She would have considerable discretion over the Texas Enterprise Fund, although recovering money already awarded would depend on the grant’s terms. Reversing the much larger property tax breaks would prove far more difficult. Those agreements are made among the company, local school districts, and the governor, who cannot simply terminate them over a change in policy. State law does allow the governor to revoke the incentives if a company fails to meet certain employment or wage requirements, but even then, the company must be given an opportunity to remedy or challenge the violation. To that end, Hinojosa has said she plans on reviewing Musk’s existing incentives to ensure his companies are meeting employment obligations. Those requirements can be remarkably lenient: Per the Chronicle, SpaceX needs to create just 80 jobs at its Terafab facility to meet the minimum employment threshold for the school-district tax incentives. SpaceX’s South Texas expansion Hinojosa’s victory could also throw a wrench into SpaceX’s expansion plans in South Texas, where the company is pursuing massive new infrastructure projects—and seeking additional land for its operations. For starters, there’s the $24 billion data center and natural gas-fired power plant planned near its Starbase headquarters near the border with Mexico. SpaceX confirmed the project earlier this month and notes construction activity has already created more than 3,000 jobs, though the facility is not yet operational. (That project has already encountered resistance from local officials, with Cameron County commissioners voting this week 3–2 against advancing SpaceX’s request for a 10-year, 100% property-tax abatement for the project.) Hinojosa has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center approvals until Texas lawmakers enact stronger protections for water supplies, electricity customers, and surrounding communities. And she’s also indicated that projects already underway wouldn’t necessarily be exempt: “If it needs a permit that the state has to approve, then that’s on hold,” she told the Chronicle last week. Again, though, SpaceX has gotten a head start. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality this week approved an air permit for a natural gas plant associated with the project. But that permit covers only the power-generating component, not the entire $24 billion development. So Hinojosa could still hold up the project if SpaceX needs additional state approvals once she takes office. Meanwhile, SpaceX has also been pursuing a deal to acquire state-owned parkland near its Boca Chica launch facility, at the mouth of the Rio Grande. Texas Monthly reported last month that state officials were considering selling 1,300 acres to the company, raising obvious questions around coastal access and habitat preservation. Hinojosa, who grew up in nearby Brownsville, asked the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department shortly after her election to hold off on any action during the transition. SpaceX has since clarified that it wants approximately 1,200 acres of public parkland surrounding its launch facility—not Boca Chica Beach itself—and says it would preserve half the property as coastal habitat. And SpaceX could face another headache at Boca Chica. Benjamin Flores, the Democrat who is the incoming Texas land commissioner, plans to challenge a 2013 law allowing temporary beach closures for rocket releases, Texas Monthly reports. And while the state Supreme Court threw out a previous challenge in June, that rejection came on procedural grounds, leaving the law’s constitutionality unresolved. A possible Tesla–SpaceX merger Tesla and SpaceX have been discussing a merger, which would bring Musk’s EV, rocket, satellite and AI businesses under one corporate roof. The state’s new Democratic leadership could throw a wrench into those plans. Texas’s incoming attorney general, Nathan Johnson, has already signaled that he intends to take a very close look at any such tie-up. “Any merger of companies of that consequence warrants tremendous scrutiny,” he told Bloomberg last week, citing concerns about corporate concentration. Johnson’s office could investigate potential antitrust violations and, if deemed warranted, challenge the merger in court. Unlike Hinojosa’s proposed data center restrictions, which could require new legislation or regulations, that authority already exists under state law.|.

Hundreds of millions of dollars later, Elon Musk has some regrets.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” the world’s richest man noted at The New York Times DealBook conference this week, reflecting on the heaps of dollars he poured into Republican campaigns nationwide during this year’s midterm elections.

But that permit covers only the power-generating component, not the entire $24 billion development. So Hinojosa could still hold up the project if SpaceX needs additional state approvals once she takes office.

Meanwhile, SpaceX has also been pursuing a deal to acquire state-owned parkland near its Boca Chica launch facility, at the mouth of the Rio Grande. Texas Monthly reported last month that state officials were considering selling 1,300 acres to the organization, raising obvious questions around coastal access and habitat preservation. Hinojosa, who grew up in nearby Brownsville, asked the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department shortly after her election to hold off on any action during the transition. SpaceX has since clarified that it wants approximately 1,200 acres of public parkland surrounding its launch facility—not Boca Chica Beach itself—and says it would preserve half the property as coastal habitat.

And SpaceX could face another headache at Boca Chica. Benjamin Flores, the Democrat who is the incoming Texas land commissioner, plans to challenge a 2013 law allowing temporary beach closures for rocket launches, Texas Monthly reports. And while the state Supreme Court threw out a previous challenge in June, that rejection came on procedural grounds, leaving the law’s constitutionality unresolved.

It has been revealed that tesla and SpaceX have been discussing a merger, which would bring Musk’s EV, rocket, satellite and AI businesses under one corporate roof. The state’s upcoming Democratic leadership could throw a wrench into those plans.

Industry observers note that texas’s incoming attorney general, Nathan Johnson, has already signaled that he intends to take a very close look at any such tie-up. “Any merger of companies of that consequence warrants tremendous scrutiny,” he told Bloomberg last week, citing concerns about corporate concentration.

It has been revealed that johnson’s office could investigate potential antitrust violations and, if deemed warranted, challenge the merger in court. Unlike Hinojosa’s proposed data center restrictions, which could require newly introduced legislation or regulations, that authority already exists under state law.|.

Peeping AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy,’ notes Meredith Whittaker, so Signal is blocking screenshots

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions.
  • AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions.
  • Sources indicate that signal is the latest platform to make changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions. Signal is the latest platform to make changes. The encrypted messaging app is preventing screenshots on any device with Apple’s iOS 27 in a bid to stop AI agents from accessing sensitive information. It will also block AI assistants from capturing screen data on Android devices. “An existential threat’ Meredith Whittaker, president of Signal Technology Foundation, the nonprofit that runs the Signal app, unveiled the change in a blog post. Whittaker pointed to how Google, Apple, and Microsoft’s “agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.” The app can now block Siri AI and turn on “screen security” as a means of preventing AI assistants from scanning information. Customers can turn off the protections, but Signal warns that this could leave messages exposed and remove the app’s privacy guarantee. Signal took similar measures last year on Windows 11 to protect messages from Microsoft Recall, a feature that periodically captures and stores screenshots of your work. Signal is fed up with a lack of AI assistant transparency The current blog post seeps with frustration at Signal’s inability to do more to protect privacy amid a lack of transparency from tech giants. “We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal—and application developers beyond—lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” indicates Whittaker. She explained that Signal has struggled due to limited information about how any of these AI agents work, being forced to do its own forensic investigations into how the “AI systems access application data.”  The blog post calls on makers of major operating systems to provide tools and information about how the AI agents work and how they can be prevented from accessing sensitive data. She further stated that apps should have a way to opt out of AI tools like screen reading without having to compromise their core utility. Whittaker issues a clear warning: “Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.”.

AI is increasingly challenging the idea of digital privacy, requiring organizations to scramble for solutions.

Sources indicate that signal is the latest platform to make changes. The encrypted messaging app is preventing screenshots on any device with Apple’s iOS 27 in a bid to stop AI agents from accessing sensitive information. It will also block AI assistants from capturing screen data on Android devices.

Meredith Whittaker, president of Signal Technology Foundation, the nonprofit that runs the Signal app, confirmed the change in a blog post.

Whittaker pointed to how Google, Apple, and Microsoft’s “agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.”.

The app can now block Siri AI and turn on “screen security” as a means of preventing AI assistants from scanning information. Customers can turn off the protections, but Signal warns that this could leave messages exposed and remove the app’s privacy guarantee.

Signal took similar measures last year on Windows 11 to protect messages from Microsoft Recall, a feature that periodically captures and stores screenshots of your work.

The current blog post seeps with frustration at Signal’s inability to do more to protect privacy amid a lack of transparency from tech giants.

“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal—and application developers beyond—lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” says Whittaker.

She explained that Signal has struggled due to limited information about how any of these AI agents work, being forced to do its own forensic investigations into how the “AI systems access application data.”.

The blog post calls on makers of major operating systems to provide tools and information about how the AI agents work and how they can be prevented from accessing sensitive data.

She further noted that apps should have a way to opt out of AI tools like screen reading without having to compromise their core utility.

Whittaker issues a clear warning: “Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.”.

Industry observers note that we know Galaxy AI subscriptions are coming soon, but the details have been kept under wraps. A newly introduced leak says Now Brief’s custom cards are the next targeted feature to be adjusted, even though it was assumed only new features would require a subscription.

When Samsung’s paid Galaxy AI plan leaked, only a couple of details were made public. For starters, the plan will reportedly cost $5/month and add latest features like Bixy Action, Daily Briefing, and Gen Video. Those new features would require a paid subscription, but existing ones would be left alone, right?

It’s a bit of both, apparently. A leaked screenshot reveals further information on the Custom Cards feature under Samsung’s Now Brief umbrella (via SamMobile). For the time being, Custom Cards are limited to three. The screenshot demonstrates Galaxy AI Premium will allow consumers to create and edit more.

Custom Cards act as a sort of task for the Galaxy AI model, making it possible for users to set up complex widgets that appear in Now Brief. That ranges from weather to health information for very specific use cases. It’s a tailored widget – useful, but far from groundbreaking.

But even with the upped Custom Card limit, Samsung’s Galaxy AI Premium subscription doesn’t appear to equate to “unlimited.” The screengrab claims this:.

Creating and editing cards uses Al Plan credits. You can only create and edit cards if you have enough credits remaining.

Credits are shared across devices signed in to your Samsung account.

Sources indicate that the Galaxy AI Premium plan will let customers buy “credit packs” on top of the $5/month subscription if they run out. It’s unclear how many credits Custom Card creation eats up.

Technically, this falls under “new feature,” since Custom Cards have long been limited. Still, it would have been nice if Samsung expanded the ability as Galaxy AI has improved in lockstep with other models.

Sources indicate that we don’t know what the majority of Galaxy AI Premium looks like beyond these few details, but we likely will soon. In any case, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has been an excellent device for those of us who hardly use Galaxy AI.
